#2826. Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’

Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.

Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm.

"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.

Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."

The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.

In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together.

Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.

The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.

Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2824. Barlow looks set for season debut with Sixers after long days, ‘miserable' weeks

Barlow looks set for season debut with Sixers after long days, 'miserable' weeks originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Dominick Barlow is on the verge of his season debut with the Sixers.

The team listed Barlow as probable for its Saturday afternoon matchup with the Bucks at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

Barlow practiced Friday and has been making clear progress in his recent on-court work recovering from an injury formally classified as a "lower back stress reaction."

He was a reliable rotation fixture last season, playing 71 regular-season games and starting 59. Barlow posted 7.7 points, 4.8 rebounds, 1.2 assists and 0.9 steals per contest in 23.8 minutes per game. The Sixers then made a common-sense call to exercise his $3.4 million option for the 2026-27 season.

The 23-year-old described his back injury as "an overuse thing."

"I guess there was an area or maybe I started my (offseason) workouts too early," he said. "I don't know what it was fully in terms of what caused it. Once it happened, it happened. Nothing I can do about it besides try to correct it and get my body feeling as good as possible."

He called the past few weeks "miserable" as he rehabbed and waited on the green light by the Sixers' training staff.

"The days just felt longer," Barlow said. "Trying to be engaged mentally, which I think I've done a good job with, but the physical aspect wasn't there. I'm somebody that's prided himself on competing, being available. Not being able to do that was hard, but I'm excited to kind of put this past me."

With LeBron James and Jaylen Brown on the team now, Barlow won't start at forward when the Sixers are at full strength.

He's still a multi-dimensional frontcourt piece for Sixers head coach Nick Nurse who may very well get substantial opportunities at backup center.

"Just cutting, playing hard, being ready to make the open shot," Barlow said. "And then I don't think you can ever have too much defensive versatility. I think that's something I can bring, try to help us be more versatile."

When Barlow checks into his first game of the season, he'll appreciate the moment.

"You don't really realize what you have until it's not there (anymore)," he said. "I'm just excited to play. …. Just playing the first stint … that's going to be the main thing I'm looking forward to."

A Sixers official said the following players were all "unrestricted" at the team's light practice:

Dean Wade (left hamstring soreness/tightness)

Bona still needs to practice with contact before a return is on the table, according to the official. Saturday's game will mark his eighth consecutive absence.

Brown and Wade have both been ruled out for the 13-3 Sixers' meeting with the 1-15 Bucks. Maxey was listed as questionable Friday night.

#2821. Fan dies after falling during a fight at 49ers-Cowboys game

A man who attended Sunday’s game between the 49ers and Cowboys has died due to injuries sustained in a fight during the game.

Via The Independent, 36-year-old Marco Narro was involved in an altercation with another fan near kickoff to the game. During the fight, Narro fell. After the incident, Narro stayed and watched the game.

During the game, he started to complain about pain. He and a friend sought attention from paramedics after the game. Narro was then transported to a local hospital.

On Wednesday, Narro died. An autopsy is pending.

The Arlington Police Department has opened a formal investigation. The prevalence of security cameras at AT&T Stadium should be useful when it comes to reconstructing the events.

The situation underscores one of the basic risks of engaging in fights at sporting events. It doesn’t take much to suffer, or to inflict, a very serious injury.

#2820. Two Washington Huskies Ruled Out For Home Finale Vs Indiana

Washington will officially be without veteran running back Trey Cooley and key special teams gunner Devin Hyde this Saturday when the team hosts No. 8 Indiana in its final home game of 2026.

Cooley, a sixth-year transfer addition for the Huskies this past offseason, is set to miss his second consecutive game after suffering a concussion late in UW's 28-25 defeat against Penn State on November 7. Prior to that, the 5-foot-11, 210-pound Raleigh, North Carolina native suffered a shoulder injury in the fourth quarter at Purdue when he ran for a season-high 113 yards, half of which came on an early fourth quarter 53-yard touchdown run, in the 38-26 victory over the Boilermakers.

Coach Jedd Fisch said Monday that the ex-Troy, Georgia Tech, and Louisville runner would miss Saturday's game against the Hoosiers as he remained in concussion protocol, and made it official Friday as Cooley was downgraded to out after being previously listed as doubtful on the final Big Ten availability report prior to the last game day report that will be released two hours before kickoff Saturday.

Hyde, a 6-foot-6, 225-pound reserve edge rusher and special teamer, had made 23 straight appearances in his first two seasons for the Huskies before being ruled out for the Week 11 contest against IU. The Menlo-Atherton star and former three-star recruit in the 2025 recruiting class has been listed on UW's availability report the past two weeks due to an undisclosed injury.

While Hyde and Cooley won't make an appearance in the 2026 home finale, UW is expected to have veteran edge rusher Logan George, an Ohio State transfer, available again opposite fourth-year starter Jacob Lane.

George has only been listed on the Huskies' availability reports twice this season prior to this weekend, first against Minnesota and last Saturday against the Spartans. In both instances the Pocatello, Idaho native ultimately suited up for second-year defensive coordinator Ryan Walters after missing UW's 48-16 victory against Eastern Washington.

On the visiting sideline will be two key Indiana starters on defense, fourth-year cornerback AJ Harris and third-year linebacker Rolijah Hardy, who were also ruled out for the Hoosiers' road test at UW with separate injuries. Harris was also listed on IU's availability report leading up to last Saturday's game against USC before he was deemed healthy enough to play in the 27-13 win for Curt Cignetti, which saw the ex-Penn State standout make 7 tackles and log 53 snaps against the Trojans.

Hardy did not play for the Hoosiers in their Week 10 victory and will miss his third straight game after being a crucial defender this season, with 5.5 tackles for loss over the first eight games in 2026.

#2819. Game Preview: Knicks vs Trail Blazers, November 21, 2026

As we all know, Madison Square Garden isn't just the most glorious gymnasium on the planet and revered in the world of sports; it's also famous for the long list of famous musicians who have performed under its unique bicycle-wheel ceiling. Now the Portland Trail Blazers are dropping by for a quick game of hoops on Saturday night, but they might actually be the one franchise that would be adept at bringing out the microphones as well. I mean, who wouldn't want to hear the newest rendition of all-timers like "Bust A Bucket" or "Rip City Rhapsody"?!

Not to disappoint anybody, but the days of Terry Porter and those shiny lycra dance outfits of the Blazers cheerleaders that would have made Cory Everson proud are long gone. Today's Rip City Rascals (coming in at 10-5) have their own way of entertaining a crowd, though, which is more than many would have expected before the season. With the return of Damian Lillard and a highly questionable move for "Pistol Petey" Ja Morant, the Blazers looked to be about five years late to the modern NBA party but atleast early it turns out they are anything but.

New head coach Micah Nori is making one of the more funky-looking rosters in the Association work so far, and he does it with a very modern, analytical approach. The Blazers shoot and make way more threes than their opponents (outscoring them by about 12+ points from beyond the arc), defend downtown better than 25 other teams in the NBA, and make sure Tony Brothers and his brothers-in-arms in the striped shirts have a living by drawing the second most fouls in the league.

Most of those foul numbers might be attributed to Deni Avdija. Only Luka from the Lakers and that feaky Greek in Miami stand at the charity stripe more frequently than the Israeli All-Star from Portland, leading to some fans questioning the ethics in his basketball bravado. But make no mistake about it, he is a serious talent, big-bodied and confident with a well-rounded game that can give every opponent problems. If he will be of any concern to the Knicks is not clear yet though; Avdija missed Portland's last two with a foot injury and figures to be a game-time decision.

But even without Avdija, Portland (road record 7-3) will present a very interesting matchup for your Knickerbockers. Damian Lillard seems to be rejuvenated after his Achilles injury, and a lot about his game feels a bit more wholesome in the jersey in which he always belonged. Behind him you have a Jrue Holiday coming off the bench, probably one of the more professional, classy guys you can find in the NBA these days. Cheekily, he also still packs quite a punch in his game, giving Nori first-class playmaking, tough D, and leadership in spades. If you think rattling these two old wily pros might get you anywhere, think again.

You could have more luck with some of the younger Blazers, but many of them bring certain elite skills to the table, too. Belgian baller Toumani Camara is one of the best defenders in the entire league, long, lanky, and extremely athletic. Seemingly plodding big man Donovan Clingan is getting more mobile by the minute and still hasn't lost his knack for gobbling up boards like a motivated Moses Malone did back in the day. Sidy Cissoko is another promising young wing, and former number two overall pick Scoot Henderson, while having a nightmarish season overall, can still break out for a big one as he did against Milwaukee the other night with 27 points.

What all those Blazers have in common is that they buy into Nori's system so far and operate with a clear-cut plan on the shiny hardwood. They extend their defense, making it hard to find anything downtown but also possible to do some damage in the midrange. On offense, they move the ball well, play five-out as much as they can (using Clingan as a high screen setter), and rely on balanced scoring night in and night out. It's a good formula, especially without Ja Morant, who has missed all but four games with a hamstring injury so far this year. The Knicks will have to touch the paint plenty to get that Portland defense moving, and they have to attack Lillard whenever possible on that end. Their superior depth could be a factor as well.

If the Blazers then throw a curveball and try to actually upend the Knicks' three-game winning streak by dragging them into a singing competition after all? No need to worry – we still got Tyler Kolek!

#2816. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2815. Know Your Foe: Oklahoma Sooners vs. Texas A&M Aggies

The Oklahoma Sooners will be at home again in Week 12, with a record of 6-4 overall and 4-3 in the SEC. Head coach Brent Venables and his team won consecutive games for the first time all season last week, and they're looking to make it three straight victories this week.

OU's season began with a win over UTEP, which was followed by a loss to Michigan. The Sooners beat New Mexico, but then lost to Georgia. After the bye week, Oklahoma beat Texas, but then lost to Kentucky. A win over Mississippi State was followed up by a loss to South Carolina. Then the Sooners defeated Florida and Ole Miss in succession, setting up this weekend.

Saturday will see the Texas A&M Aggies come to Norman. They went 11-2 last season, winning 11 straight games to open the regular season, before losing to Texas in the finale and Miami at home in the first round of the College Football Playoff.

Head coach Mike Elko is in his third season in College Station, after the Aggies hired him away from his post as Duke's head coach following the 2023 season to replace Jimbo Fisher. Before his two years with the Blue Devils, Elko had been on Fisher's staff at Texas A&M as the defensive coordinator for four years. He's held the same role at both Wake Forest and Notre Dame in the last decade.

Elko's Aggies are struggling in 2026, entering this game with a 4-6 overall record and a 1-6 mark in the SEC. The year started well, with wins over Missouri State (50-0) and Arizona State (48-20), but losses to Kentucky (31-21) and LSU (35-6) followed. The Aggies beat Arkansas (34-7), lost to Missouri (27-6), and defeated The Citadel (41-0), but have now lost three straight games. Texas A&M fell to Alabama (31-20), South Carolina (17-9), and Tennessee (22-7) over the last few weeks.

Both schools are enduring disappointing seasons after playoff trips last year, but where the Sooners have found something over the last two weeks, the Aggies have seen a rough year get rougher over the last three games.

On offense, the struggling Aggies are led by offensive coordinator Holmon Wiggins. He'll be matched up against Venables, who calls the plays for OU's defense. However, Venables said after last week's win that it's a "collaboration" with his defensive staff when it comes to play-calling, after some believed he wasn't calling the plays late in the game against the Rebels. Venables' top assistant on defense is Todd Bates, who coaches OU's defensive tackles.

Wiggins was Texas A&M's wide receivers coach for the last two years, after serving in the same capacity at Alabama for five seasons before coming to Aggieland. Wiggins was promoted after former OC Collin Klein left to become Kansas State's head coach.

The Aggies have been poor offensively with Wiggins at the controls this season, falling off dramatically from last year. Marcel Reed has been the starting quarterback all year, but Texas A&M appears to be making a change to backup Brady Hart as the starter this week. He's less of a dual-threat than Reed is, but the Aggies are hoping he can give the unit a spark.

Running back Reuben Owens II is the team's leading rusher, but Texas A&M has a number of backs who have earned carries. K.J. Edwards, Carsyn Baker, and Jamarion Morrow have all scored multiple touchdowns this season. Wide receivers Isaiah Horton, Mario Craver, and Aaron Gregory are the players to watch in the passing game this week.

On the other side of the ball, OU interim offensive coordinator Jason Witten will be matched up against a very strong unit that is the strength of Texas A&M's team. Witten has been solid since taking over the offense after Venables made the decision to fire former offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle. On the other sideline, Elko has a deep defensive background, and he began the season calling the plays. However, he handed those duties off to defensive coordinator Lyle Hemphill midseason. Elijah Robinson is the co-defensive coordinator for the Aggies.

Hemphill was promoted to DC ahead of this season after former DC Jay Bateman left for the same role and control of the defense at Kentucky. Hemphill has a long history with Elko, but he was James Madison's defensive coordinator in 2024. Robinson was in College Station for the Fisher era, but spent the last two seasons at Syracuse as the defensive coordinator. He's back working under Elko for his second stint in 2026.

In just his third collegiate game as a play-caller, Witten will be trying to make quarterback John Mateer comfortable against everything Elko, Hemphill, and Robinson are going to throw at him. Defensive end Marco Jones leads the Aggies in sacks, while linebacker Ray Coney and safety Dalton Brooks are the squad's leading tacklers. OU's offense has found an identity over the last two weeks, and it has consisted of a strong commitment to running the ball, dominating time of possession, and setting Mateer up to do what he does best. It's unlikely that the plan is going to change that much, especially in a game featuring two good defenses that figures to be low-scoring.

OU special teams coordinator Doug Deakin will face off against Texas A&M special teams coordinator Patrick Dougherty this week. Dougherty was with Elko at Duke, and he followed him to Texas A&M ahead of the 2024 season. Texas A&M has had strong special teams under Dougherty, while Deakin's unit did not have a good day last week. Kicker Tate Sandell has been inconsistent this year, and he missed two field goals against the Rebels. OU also had a punt partially blocked, and muffed a late onside kick. Some of that was due to the poor weather in the re-scheduled Sunday afternoon game against Ole Miss, but with rain in the forecast in Norman again this week, Oklahoma's special teams unit has to play a lot better than they did last week to win this game.

Of course, Oklahoma and Texas A&M were former Big 12 foes, and they're facing off for the first time as SEC foes this season. OU owns a 19-12 series lead, and the Sooners have an 11-3 record against the Aggies since 1999. The last meeting between the two teams came in the Cotton Bowl for the 2012 season, with Texas A&M dominating in a 41-13 win. The most recent meeting as conference opponents and the most recent meeting in Norman was in 2011, a game OU won 41-25.

Oklahoma has had some iconic moments against Texas A&M, such as linebacker Torrance Marshall's game-winning pick-six in 2000 in College Station, saving the eventual-champion Sooners in a 35-31 win. In 2003 in Norman, OU won 77-0, completely overwhelming the Aggies to the point that they had to stop scoring in order to not run it up on Texas A&M.

Neither team has had the season they expected to have this year, and neither team has put a very functional offense on the field for the majority of this season. However, the Sooners have become bowl-eligible with impressive wins over the last two weeks, and they've found something that has been working for them on offense. Both teams hang their hat on their defense, with two defensive-minded head coaches at the helm. This game has the potential to be a rock fight, and it's hard to see a lot of points being scored on Saturday.

Texas A&M needs to win its final two games to get to bowl eligibility, and with three straight losses and just one SEC win, the Aggies are desperate, and their backs are against the wall. Oklahoma is looking to find a strong finish to a rocky season, and with bowl eligibility already accomplished, the focus turns to making a better bowl game with wins down the stretch.

The Aggies defense makes this game dangerous, as it's the best unit the Witten-led OU offense has seen so far. However, that offense should get its fair share of chances, as Oklahoma's defense certainly has the ability to cause problems for Texas A&M's offense.

Anytime you're playing a wounded and hungry team, the potential for an unexpected result is always there, especially against a roster as talented as Texas A&M's. On the other hand, if Oklahoma can continue its better play, the third-most wins in the Venables era could be accomplished this week. Winning out and getting to eight victories would look much better than finishing with six or seven victories, but the Sooners can't win eight games until they win a seventh game. It isn't the season anyone at OU wanted, but eight wins (and four straight) would signal definite improvement after a 4-4 record through the first two months.

Kickoff for Oklahoma-Texas A&M is scheduled for 2:45 p.m. CT in Norman on Saturday on ESPN2.

#2813. As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive

As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.

Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

#2811. ‘It worked every time': How Sixers found a clutch answer at shootaround

'It worked every time': How Sixers found a clutch answer at shootaround originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers created their two cleanest late-game looks several hours before they needed them.

During Wednesday morning's shootaround in Orlando, Nick Nurse had the Sixers work on offensive material they had not consistently used this season. They tested one of those actions during the first half, returned to it throughout the closing minutes and watched it produce the shots they needed to complete a 17-point comeback.

"We worked on some stuff this morning that we hadn't used before, and they ran all that stuff very, very well and very calmly and with composure," Nurse told reporters.

The Sixers have earned six of their 13 wins after trailing by double digits. They are also 11-0 in games that reached clutch time.

Relying on comebacks is not a sustainable plan. The repeated late-game situations, however, have forced a new roster to respond to different lineups, coverages and responsibilities while the season is still young.

Each close finish gives Nurse more information about which players and actions hold up when possessions tighten. Wednesday gave him a new option.

Anfernee Simons' clinching three in the Sixers' 121-116 win over the Magic was the final result of that preparation.

"That last play, we ran that play in the first half," Simons said. "We worked it a couple of times, and in the second half we ran that play every single time down the stretch, and it worked every time.

"It was a play we ran through. [It's gratifying] especially when it's working consistently and you're getting different shots out of it and the opposing team just don't know what to do.

"We just continue to run the play and get the open shots we need."

NBC Sports Philadelphia video producer and Sixers Talk podcast co-host Kevin Rice broke down how the Sixers used its different options to keep Orlando guessing.

The action begins with two players stationed near the elbows. A player on the opposite elbow then sets a screen for the player up top, who receives the ball while moving around it.

The Sixers ran the set three consecutive times during the first half. None of the possessions reached the primary option. Each still produced a quality opportunity.

On the first, Joel Embiid cleared LeBron James out of the area and directed Simons around him for a dribble handoff. Simons received an open three-point look.

Orlando took away the handoff the next time down but left Embiid one-on-one against Wendell Carter Jr. Embiid created enough room to retrieve his own miss and convert an and-one opportunity.

The third attempt pulled Orlando's defense into the paint. Two passes moved the ball through the collapsing coverage and created an open three for VJ Edgecombe.

"We had a little thing where he comes flying off behind Joel, and he doesn't get to do that that much, right?" Nurse said of Simons. "So tonight he gets the opportunity to do it, and it was very good for us on a number of plays."

The Sixers changed the action late without abandoning its initial Horns alignment. Simons moved through the lane to help form a Spain pick-and-roll involving James and Embiid.

On the first late possession, Simons remained near the play after James gained a matchup against Carter. Orlando struggled to sort out its assignments, leaving James open for a 19-foot jumper with 54.8 seconds remaining.

After Jalen Suggs made one of two free throws, the Sixers returned to the same setup. This time, Simons relocated to the left corner after James drew Carter on a switch.

James drove into the paint. Suggs lost track of Simons while responding to the penetration, and James sent the ball toward the corner.

Simons buried the open three to give the Sixers a 119-113 lead with 15 seconds left.

"Bron just penetrated the paint," Simons said. "It kind of got some confusion, and when I was on the dunker and kind of spaced out to the corner, I ended up finding myself wide open for the three, and Bron found me."

The Sixers entered the night without Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown, their two leading scorers. Simons made his first start with Philadelphia and recorded 18 points in the city where he grew up.

His final basket also illustrated why Nurse believes the Sixers have more to uncover with him.

"When he's out there, they gotta be really careful," Nurse said. "So I think there's some drives he creates, and just about every time he lets it go, whether he's on balance or not, you think it's going in, and that is a big deal. Like, that is a big deal.

"And again, I think we're still a ways away from really unlocking him to being even more part of some of the things we can do with him to create more shots."

Philadelphia is now 11-0 in clutch games. The finish in Orlando provided a more specific explanation than experience or shot-making alone.

The Sixers installed a set in the morning, explored its counters and trusted it when the game tightened. James supplied the patience to read Orlando's coverage. Embiid occupied the middle of the action. Simons moved without the ball, and Edgecombe remained ready to shoot.

James said his heart rate drops when close games increase the pressure on everyone else.

"I mean, experience," James said. "A guy that's seen every situation this league has to offer. It's nothing I haven't seen. And, you know, in the moments where people's heart rate goes up or anxiety goes up, mine is pretty low. It's actually lower, you know."

The Sixers still have more actions and reads to learn as Nurse becomes familiar with his new personnel, but their latest win showed their innate ability to adapt in big moments.

"I think we're still a long ways away from knowing all the reads and all that stuff because it's just a little early, right?" Nurse said.

#2810. Commanders HC Dan Quinn praises rookie LB Sonny Styles as a blitzer

The Washington Commanders have found themselves a generational talent in linebacker Sonny Styles, who fell to them as the No. 7 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. As a rookie, Styles has been the best defender for the Commanders so far.

He leads Washington in total tackles with 80 and is on track to have over 150 tackles this season. Styles also leads the Commanders in solo tackles with 37 and is tied for second in tackles for loss with five. An underrated aspect of his game has been his ability to blitz as Styles has at least seven blitzes in four games this season, including Washington's most recent win against the New York Giants.

"I wasn't as aware of how good a blitzer he was going to be. I thought he would, but he didn't do it as much at Ohio State. So to see that part of his game come to life, that's also been good," head coach Dan Quinn told Cris Collinsworth. "But I think what, for me coaching him, to see the attention to detail that he wants to have, the professionalism, his constant searching for improvement. That, to me, is what jumps out, his humility, his willingness to work. He's going on the way up and it's already at a good level. So, I'm excited to see where he can take it. He's got good instincts. He made a fantastic play at the end of the game [against the Giants], but I loved his remark afterward just as much. In the first game, he commented they did this on third and three. I thought something would be different in that spot. So, here's a guy applying what he learned from the first game against the Giants and then put it into the second game. So, he's been an excellent addition for us."

With how well he has played this season, Styles should certainly be a finalist for Defensive Rookie of the Year. He will have an opportunity to continue to bolster his resume on Monday Night Football against one of the NFL's best offenses, the Cincinnati Bengals.

#2809. 3 Keys to Victory for Ravens-Panthers in Week 11

This is it. You can't finish with a record of 11-6 until you first reach 5-6. Technically, the Ravens could make the playoffs with seven or eight losses — but this feels like a defining moment. With the Houston Texans on the rise, Tampa Bay's roster built perfectly to beat the Ravens, and then four division games in a row, this game against Carolina feels like the easiest one remaining on the schedule. If the Ravens lose, any little fleeting hope for a run will fizzle. It's been a drama-filled week for the Ravens, and they'll be missing Nnamdi Madubuike, so they need to figure out how to put their heads down and grind out this win to avoid dropping six in a row.

The Ravens have run multiple tight end sets at the seventh-highest rate this year, 43.6% of the time, according to Next Gen Stats. They are largely successful throwing out of these sets as well, averaging 8.1 yards per pass attempt, which is 12th-most in the league. The issue is they pass out of 12 and 13 personnel less than 40% of the time, according to SumerSports. This both inflates their pass success rate and shows they are running more than 60% of the time out of these formations, allowing defenses to key in on the run. Recently, Declan Doyle has had an issue with running out of heavy on first down too frequently, making it very obvious and setting the Ravens behind the chains.

The Ravens need to start mixing it up more. That could mean throwing out of heavy on early downs more often to catch the Panthers by surprise. The biggest issue there is that the Panthers have allowed the third-fewest yards per attempt against multi-tight end sets (5.8). The real solution might just be to lean on Jacoby Brissetts arm, play more 11 personnel, and sling the ball around the field to Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman and Ja'Kobi Lane. The Panthers have been down their top three cornerbacks for a while. Rookie Will Lee is expected to return in this one, but Jaycee Horn remains on IR and Mike Jackson, while practicing this week, hasn't been activated yet. The Ravens might want to test whoever is covering their wide receivers. Spreading the offense out in 11 might help the run game as well if the Ravens can find success early through the air and back the Panthers off the line of scrimmage and out of the box.

Hendrickson leads the Ravens in pressures despite missing two games and dealing with a figure injury since Week 1. He's also getting double-teamed 42% of his pass rush snaps, according to ESPN. He also only has two sacks through his first eight games as a Raven, and that simply isn't good enough or what the Ravens paid for. Conversely, the Ravens have seen Green get better throughout this season while going through some ups and downs, switching from one side of the defensive front to the other. He leads the Ravens in sacks with 5.5. The Panthers' biggest overall weakness is their offensive line.

Both of Carolina's offensive tackles have been question marks this season. Their rookie right tackle, Monroe Freeling, has a 6-foot-7 frame with speed and athleticism, but the transition from left tackle in college to right in the NFL hasn't been without questions. Rasheed Walker on the left side has struggled this season and given up a chunk of sacks as well. Without Madubuike, the Ravens need their two top edge rushers to get pressures and, more importantly, finish.

It's no surprise to anyone who watches Ravens games that their defense has given up a lot over the middle of the field. They've also been the worst defense on intermediate passes, giving up a league-worst 0.77 EPA per play on passes between 10 and 19 yards. Furthermore, the Ravens have been targeted on in-breaking routes on 36.7% of opponents' passes, giving up seven touchdowns on them, 10th most in the league according to Next-Gen Stats. Meanwhile, the Panthers have four different 6-foot-4 wide receivers, and Bryce Young has thrown in-breakers on 38.8% of his routes, averaging 9.0 yards per attempt on these routes. That's a lot of size and a lot of attempts for Roquan Smith to cover over the middle.

Jesse Minter's defense is designed to leave the middle of the field open; it's the hardest area of the field to consistently throw in, with the most bodies, hands, arms, and heads to navigate. The idea is to funnel passes there, force as many tough throws as possible, and then have 11 hats on the ball to tackle quickly when passes do get caught there. It hasn't worked so far. The Ravens players haven't executed it consistently all season, and Minter has yet to deviate from it. Something has to change, and this would be a great game to make changes for it.

#2805. 3 things from Charlotte's 111-97 loss to Atlanta

The Charlotte Hornets suffered another loss Friday night, as the Atlanta Hawks eliminated them from NBA Cup contention. Although the Hornets led at halftime, their effort couldn't be sustained, as Atlanta outscored Charlotte 31-19 in the third quarter. From there, the Hawks were well in control, extending their lead as high as 19 points, ultimately earning a 111-97 victory.

Moussa Diabate was dominant for the away team, as the Frenchman tied a career-high with 21 points to go along with 15 rebounds, two assists and one steal on 9-for-12 shooting. Naz Reid also had a double-double, tallying 12 points and 10 rebounds, while Brandon Miller scored 19 points. All-Star Jalen Johnson stole the show for Atlanta, finishing with 26 points, six rebounds, six assists and four steals. Ahead of Charlotte's next matchup against the Grizzlies, here are three things to take note of as the season progresses.

The Charlotte Hornets missed six of their 16 free-throw attempts Friday night, as Naz Reid, Moussa Diabate and Sion James missed a pair each. Free-throw shooting has been a strength for Charlotte this season, shooting 81.4% from the line, third-best in the NBA. Grayson Allen is shooting 92.7% from the stripe, while rookie Christian Anderson Jr. has yet to miss a foul shot.

In a game where Jalen Johnson and Dyson Daniels tallied four steals each, the Hornets finished with one block and four steals for the entire game. In 15 contests to begin the season, the Hornets rank 25th in blocks per game and 29th in steals per game. Although shooting is at the core of Charlotte's playstyle, they could afford to add a defensive stopper on the perimeter.

Despite hoisting 12 fewer attempts, the Hawks finished with more made 3-pointers than Charlotte. Now 15 games in, the Hornets attempt the most 3-pointers per game (45.4) but remain dead last in 3-point percentage (31%). While offensive rebounding can often keep the Hornets within striking distance of their opponents, shooting will have to improve to end Charlotte's four-game losing streak.

#2803. Daiyan Henley being out with a knee injury changes nothing about the failed trade to Broncos

The failed trade of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley returned to the front burner on Friday, with the news that Henley will miss Sunday's game against the Jets due to a knee injury.

It was a knee condition that prompted the Broncos to pull the plug on the deal — after trying to renegotiate the terms after the trade deadline.

From Mike Klis of 9News, who covers the Broncos: "Chargers ILB Daiyan Henley missed entire week of practices with knee injury and has been ruled out for game vs Jets. This validates concerns raised by Broncos medical team and GM George Paton. And proves Chargers were not on the up and up."

Does it really prove that the Chargers weren't "on the up and up"? The issue is that the Denver physical flagged a knee problem. In lieu of finding that the physical had been failed and that the trade won't happen, the Broncos were willing to give Henley a passing grade, if the compensation was changed.

Henley has played every game this season. He played on Monday night against the Ravens. As far as anyone knows, he injured the knee during that game.

As far as anyone knows, the currently injured knee isn't the same knee that created the concern during the Denver physical.

It's all just noise at this point. The core problem is the ability of a team — after the trade deadline has passed — to renegotiate the terms of a trade. And the related issue is the ability of a team to give a conditional grade on the pass-fail question of a physical that is tied to the specific compensation.

A player either passes the physical, or he fails it. The process shouldn't include an epilogue premised on the outcome of the physical being "maybe." Especially after the time for negotiating trades has ended.

#2802. Observations after Sixers come back for strong shorthanded victory

Observations after Sixers come back for strong shorthanded victory originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stretched their winning streak to four games and snagged a strong road win Wednesday night over the Magic.

They earned a 121-116 victory in Orlando to improve to 13-3 on the season. The Magic dropped to 6-8.

Joel Embiid had 26 points, seven assists, six rebounds, three blocks and two steals.

VJ Edgecombe posted a season-high 24 points, eight boards and six assists.

LeBron James scored 22 points and Anfernee Simons added 18.

Magic star Franz Wagner had 27 points, 11 assists and eight rebounds.

The Sixers had a long injury list in Orlando. Tyrese Maxey (right foot soreness), Jaylen Brown (left hamstring strain) and Dean Wade (left hamstring soreness/tightness) were among their players out. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse told reporters in Orlando that Brown will be re-evaluated when the team returns to Philadelphia.

Orlando was without star forward Paolo Banchero (right high ankle sprain).

The Sixers will start a three-game homestand when they face the Bucks on Saturday afternoon. Here are observations on their win over the Magic:

The Sixers' undermanned starting lineup was Edgecombe, Simons, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, James and Embiid.

After scoring 37 points in the Sixers' win over the Nets, Embiid had a subpar start. He began 1 for 6 from the floor and committed a turnover that led to an Anthony Black dunk.

The Sixers' lineup looked exactly like a unit that hadn't built any chemistry yet. The team was not sharp early on either end of the floor.

Desmond Bane drained a long three-pointer to give Orlando a 27-12 advantage. Orlando made 11 of its first 14 field goals and led by as many as 17 points in the first quarter.

Labaron Philon Jr. and Justin Edwards joined the Sixers' rotation. So did two-way contract players Tacko Fall and Caleb Love.

Philon impressed in the first quarter, converting two floaters and a corner three. The rookie passed his previous NBA scoring high of five points and finished the night with 10 on 4-for-5 shooting.

Fall played 10 minutes and posted two points, three rebounds and three blocks. He slammed in a dunk and rejected two shots early in the second quarter. Credit to Fall for giving the Sixers a good backup center performance and doing his job as a rim-protecting ultra-big man.

Love entered in the second quarter and was ready to fire, hitting a catch-and-shoot three-pointer on his first touch.

The Sixers' zone defense also helped them eat into the Magic's lead. The zone seemed to disrupt Orlando's offensive rhythm and it was active enough to prevent the Magic from consistently creating high-quality looks.

Edgecombe's buzzer-beating mid-range jumper cut the Sixers' deficit to 69-64 after two quarters.

The Sixers pulled within a single point on multiple occasions in the third quarter, including on a Philon three late in the period. They trailed by five points after the third.

Fall continued to play well early in the fourth quarter. He deterred the Magic's drivers from getting all the way to the rim as the very large back line of the Sixers' zone defense and made eye-catching hustle plays on both sides of the ball.

The Sixers outscored Orlando by seven points on the night with Fall on the court. Soon after Embiid subbed back in, he evened the game at 104-all with two free throws. Jabari Walker swished a three to finally push the Sixers in front.

The Magic regained a late lead with a Jalen Suggs three. James then drove and kicked the ball out to Edgecombe, who nailed one of his customary clutch jumpers to put the Sixers back on top.

No matter the night-to-night personnel, the Sixers have been fantastic at the tail end of close games. They're now 11-0 in clutch situations, which the NBA defines as games within a five-point differential in the final five minutes.

#2797. Rockets sputter late in Denver 133-124

Tonight featured the Rockets third NBA Cup game, which was essentially a must-win after their opening NBA Cup round loss to Dallas. The Rockets would be playing in Denver, against a Nuggets team that seems to be finding its way after initially scuffling this season.

Many have mocked and derided the NBA Cup, and sure, it's a gimmick, and it's artificial, and so forth. But the sad truth is, professional sports are a gimmick, and are artificial, too. This is just a new wrinkle in the existing structure, not some sort of attack on the traditional and pure nature of NBA basketball. But even if you think it is some sort of assault, don't you want to watch players trying their hardest, during the regular season? Because they do try hard. These games actually are extra, because hyper competitive NBA players like being hyper competitive. It took a few years, but the players are there, they mean it (at least in the early games). By the time a 14 year old NBA fan today is in their mid 20s, the NBA Cup will always have been part of the NBA for them.

Anyhow, the Rockets won't be moving on in the NBA Cup this year. It's possible to move on with 3 wins, but not with maybe 2. Those who don't like this added competition are free to celebrate this.

As for tonight, there are two ways of looking at it.

The Rockets were on their fifth consecutive road game, which happened to be an NBA Cup game, at altitude in Denver. Denver is where good road trips go to die, and if they don't die there, it'll happen in Salt Lake City (you can look it up).

On top of the schedule, and the location, a bunch of player who had previously been kind of bad for Denver so far this season had excellent night. Aaron Gordon, Cam Johnson, and Christian Braun went 20-29 and threw in another 11 points from free throws, which they shot at 10-11.

The Rockets on the other hand, missed 12 free throws out of 35 attempts, shooting 66% to Denver's 93%.

The Rockets bench played 75 minutes and managed all of 12 points.

The Denver bench played 75 minutes as well, and contributed 37 points.

The game featured over 40 lead changes, and was anyone's game until the mid 4th quarter.

Maybe the altitude told on the Rockets starters, and Denver's stars, Jokic and Murray, whom the Rockets had held down most of the first half, came alive.

The duel between Sengun and Jokic was pretty much a dead heat individually.

Jokic went 10-15/2-3 3pt/7 rbs/11 ast/4 To for 26 points.

Sengun went 9-16/1-2 3pt/11 rbs/10 ast/2 TO/1 stl/1 blk for 28 points.

This one was painful, but not unexpected.

The second way is a little more alarming:

The Rockets held a narrow lead towards the end of a high scoring game. They couldn't keep scoring, and lost it.

As the game got tighter late, Denver clamped down on defense, and the Rockets simply couldn't execute offense.

The Rocket with the most shots was Fred VanVleet. This wasn't due to setting up Fred for shots, it was due to Fred often finding no passes, no one really doing much of anything, and being forced to take a late clock attempt.

FVV did this pretty well, but he also shot the most shots on the team, at 21, and was part of the Rockets two guards (including Amen) going 4-11 from the free throw line.

Kevin Durant took 9 shots, wasn't assertive and the Rockets couldn't get him the ball late, anyway.

Jabari Smith was on fire, but only got 8 attempts, of which he made 7.

The late game collapse, and it was a collapse in the final minutes, felt very familiar. Unable to get stops. Unable to execute on offense. There was no plan, no special action to get the Rockets best offensive players tonight, Sengun, and Jabari Smith, looks late. It was, again, a lot of Fred VanVleet dribbling under pressure, and often making a difficult midrange shot with no time remaining.

The level of competition was high, the level of intensity of that competition was high, so it's not unreasonable to have concerns about this outcome. Denver might be a first round playoff opponent, for example.

One game doesn't make a trend, and isn't proof of anything, but I saw in this game a painful reminder of painful games last season. That could just be bad memories, and sensitivity to certain sorts of issues. The season, and especially the playoffs, will tell us.

#2796. Interview with the Enemy: Chicago Bears

This week, the New Orleans Saints will head to Solider Field to face the Chicago Bears in Week 11 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Bill Zimmerman of Windy City Gridiron joins us to preview this weekend's matchup.

NJ: How legitimate are the Bears' Super Bowl aspirations at this point in the season? Does it feel like this could finally be the year Chicago gets it done?

BZ: The Jeffery Simmons trade changed everything as far as I'm concerned. The Bears defense was the reason they weren't a true Super Bowl contender. Dennis Allen was largely doing it with smoke and mirrors. Yes, he had really effective blitz packages on 3rd down, but that wasn't sustainable in the playoffs against great teams.

The offense was never a question; the defense was. With Simmons, he's a multiplier. In just two games, we've seen the play improve of every defensive lineman and linebacker around him. If their front 7 can play like this, it will help a banged-up secondary that is the weakest part of the team.

No one can guarantee a Super Bowl, but I do think the Bears are on the short list of true Super Bowl contenders this year (and that's very foreign to write).

NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Bears on Sunday against the Saints? Is there a particular area in which New Orleans could exploit?

BZ: The Bears are the healthiest they've been in a while heading into this game. They have RB Kyle Monangai returning, which will be a huge boost for their running game, and rookie CB Malik Muhammad may not be the biggest name, but he is a key starter in their secondary.

TE Cole Kmet is out for the year, and S Coby Bryant has been out since training camp. The only other notable starter who will be out is CB Kyler Gordon, who injured his shoulder against Tampa; he did finish the game, but he is now listed as out for this one.

The key to stopping the Bears is to attack their cornerbacks. It's the weakest part of the roster, but you have to make sure you are getting the ball out quickly before Jeffery Simmons collapses the pocket.

NJ: How much of an impact has Dennis Allen had on turning around the Bears' defense throughout his tenure? Have there been any decisions or coaching tendencies that have rubbed fans the wrong way?

BZ: I think Dennis Allen is very popular among Bears fans, and I think he was the perfect DC hire with Ben Johnson. I think Dennis Allen is at a point where he almost certainly isn't going to get another head coaching job. That means he should be able to pair with Johnson and be the top coaches on this coaching staff for years to come. If things go well, they'll have an Andy Reid/Steve Spagnuolo type partnership.

I think, before the Simmons trade, people had been frustrated with how Dennis Allen wanted to build his defensive line, but other than that, I think Bears fans are very happy with how he calls a game, and I think most of us understand that he got a lot more success out of his defense than the level of talent that was on the field.

The best thing he's done in Chicago is create a phenomenal third down defense. The Bears have been quite strong on third downs and it's forcing teams to get big chunk plays on the early downs or end up punting the ball back to the Bears.

NJ: Who is one Bears player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance?

BZ: Offensively, I don't think there are many names to give because Caleb Williams, Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, and Rome Odunze are their main weapons, and I think football fans are pretty familiar with all of them. I do think Kyle Monangai is going to be a big part of the offensive game plan and split carries with D'Andre Swift so Monangai is one returning from injury that I think can have a strong game.

Defensively, I mentioned Muhammad, but I'll give you Austin Booker. He was a 5th-round pick in 2024 out of Missouri, and he's been coming into his own this year as an improved run defender and a solid pass rusher. You should hear Booker's name at least once on Sunday, either making a TFL or a sack.

NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook, the Bears (-720) are currently 11.5-point favorites over the Saints (+520) in Sunday's matchup; what is your final score prediction and how do you see the game playing out?

BZ: It's really hard to imagine that the Bears don't win this one. Ben Johnson is great on extra rest, and the Bears are healthy, and I don't think it's an insult to say the Bears are simply a better team than the Saints and are playing them at home. I think the question isn't who will win or whether the Bears cover the big spread?

I think the offense is going to have success regardless. I think it comes down to if you think the Saints can get points on the Bears' defense. If you do, then there's no reason to think this one couldn't be like 31 to 21 or so, and the Saints cover. #2795. NFL will consider requiring minimum-night stays for international games

After the 49ers and the Rams took dramatically different approaches to their arrival in Melbourne for the first-ever Australia game, we raised the question of whether the league should require teams to get there early enough to advance the goal of promoting American football to international audiences.

Via The Athletic, the NFL will consider adopting a minimum-night stay for teams playing internationally.

“Currently, we leave those football decisions on when the team arrives in the market to the club,” NFL executive V.P. of club business, major events, and international Peter O’Reilly told The Athletic. “It is something that we’ll consider moving forward on: Do we put some minimum nights in a market in there? It’s something we’ll look at.”

The league already does it for the Super Bowl, mandating a full-week experience that includes multiple press conferences, the annual “Opening Night” media extravaganza, and practicing at designated facilities.

“Having access to players and that type of experience when they’re in the market does have a lasting impact,” O’Reilly said. “That’s a factor when you start to think about encouraging or potentially looking at a policy where you’d want a club in the market for more than the day before.”

Beyond impacting strategic considerations, it would add to the total expense. The money would be worth it, if it further enhances the league’s overall reason for going global.

#2792. Lakers needed a little bit from everyone in win against Kings

LOS ANGELES — If Friday's 106-104 win against the Sacramento Kings was any indicator, it's as if the Lakers have played bad teams so often over the past two weeks that they've started to become one.

"That was a—a win's a win," Lakers center Walker Kessler said as he labored into his postgame presser.

But just as the trillions of cells in the human body help fight a cold, Los Angeles got (and needed) a little bit of everything from everyone to get over this Sacramento flu.

Whether it was Kessler's first 3-point attempt and make of the season, seven assists from Quentin Grimes, who yet again hit a game-sealing three, five combined offensive rebounds from Jarred Vanderbilt and Sandro Mamukelashvili off the bench or 14 points from Matisse Thybulle, the Lakers needed every bit of it.

"Certain nights, whether it's the team, how we're playing, the atmosphere of the arena, you can just be a little flat," head coach JJ Redick said. "And I thought we just had to be tougher and pick up our energy. They accepted the challenge."

Friday marks the end of a stretch of four games in six nights for the Lakers, who improved to an NBA-best 14-3 record and are one of six teams to reach the 17-game mark. Los Angeles is also tied with three other teams for most back-to-back games thus far at four.

They haven't been absent of casualties during this early war of attrition. Austin Reaves missed his fourth consecutive game with a left heel bruise he suffered against Milwaukee. That the Lakers have certainly felt the impact of playing without their second-best player is no revelation, but Luka Dončić has perhaps felt his absence the most.

Dončić, the league's leading scorer, extended his shooting slump on Friday, scoring 25 points on 2-of-9 shooting from three in another game where he was the focal point of the opposing defense every second he was on the floor. Dating back to the Milwaukee game, his shooting percentages have dipped to 41.4% from the field and 30.6% from beyond the arc.

The double-teams and blitzes he saw earlier in the season were less effective when Reaves was there to make the defense pay. But without him, the weight of the offense is much heavier on Dončić.

That's where Los Angeles's role players come in. Just as inconsistent as their roles have been so far, their impact on winning has been just as consistent. Redick said postgame that their plan in the offseason was to surround Dončić and Reaves with complementary players, and that despite having played three-quarters of a game with both of them available over their last seven games, the Lakers are 6-1.

"It's a credit to the group [for] sticking with it," Redick added. "Basketball's a game of mistakes. We played through some mistakes tonight, just like we did the other night against Charlotte. Good win. We'll take it."

The locker room is beset by these shooting slumps. Dončić, Mamu, Ziaire Williams and Jake LaRavia, among others, are simply going through one of those stretches. Redick plans to use the Lakers' forthcoming two-day break — a rarity so far this season — to ensure the team continues to stay sharp and get shots up.

After Monday's rematch against Utah, the team will enjoy another three days off before clashing with San Antonio. Just as Grimes broke through a rough start to the season, Redick believes others will come around, no matter how much a slump can weigh on someone.

To that point, as Redick recently stayed up late on the iMovie app on his phone, cooking up a two-minute highlight video of six-time major champion golfer Rory McIlroy to show his players — a video he humbly thought was "well-produced and edited" — one of McIlroy's quotes stuck with him during this trying time:

"When you're not playing well, it feels like your good game is so far away. And then once you start playing well, you realize it was never that far away to begin with."

#2791. 5 Things I Think I Think About the Miami Dolphins After Week 10

If you're looking for a silver lining after the Miami Dolphins' 24-22 loss to the Indianapolis Colts, I have good news: The franchise may have found themselves a new hero, and it's Zane Gonzalez. Here are 5 things I think I think after the head-shaking loss to the Daniel Jones-led Colts.

At Nashville's Nissan Stadium, the New York Jets just won their first Super Bowl in more than 50 years. Gang Green is celebrating: Champagne, laughter, tears. Three years earlier, the Colts had traded away the pick that became the No. 1 selection in the 2027 draft. Now the quarterback chosen with that pick has delivered New York a championship. In the on-air interview, head coach Aaron Glenn hugs his third-year superstar quarterback, yelling joyously to the cameras, "We're only here because of this guy! He put us on his back and carried us to become world champions!"

The words "world champions" echo in the brain of thirty-four-year-old Miami Subs employee Zane Gonzalez as he shuts off the black-and-white television in his parents' basement.

Zane takes in all the Miami Dolphins gear around his room – his prized foam finger from 1984, the 8-inch T.D. stuffy on his pillow – and sighs. "Where did we go wrong, T.D.?" he asks his stuffy. "How did the Jets win the Super Bowl while we're still looking for a playoff win?"

"You're right, it was that 2027 draft. That win over the Colts knocked us out of the running for the top pick in the draft! We should have been the Super Bowl winners this year!" He looks up. "T.D., I know what I must do."

Six months later, after convincing Dolphins owner Stephen Ross to invest $500 million in temporal engineering, Gonzalez steps into a prototype time machine and travels three years into the past.

His mission is simple: Convince the Dolphins to bring him on as placekicker. And then?

Most importantly: Miss against the Colts.

Make sure Miami loses enough games to stay ahead of the Colts in the draft order. Land the future franchise quarterback who would finally deliver the Dolphins' long-awaited Super Bowl title.

Sacrifice a few meaningless wins today and the Dolphins become champions tomorrow.

After all, no one would willingly miss two field goals and an extra point in a game his team lost by two … right?

Zane Gonzalez stands at South Pointe Park Pier, staring out at the Atlantic.

The day before, the Dolphins lost to the Patriots, finishing off a 2-15 season and securing the first overall pick in the upcoming draft, one win ahead of the sad sack Colts.

He turns. A little girl, maybe six years old, stands behind him in an oversized Ricky Williams jersey. She clutches her well-loved T.D. stuffed dolphin under one arm.

The girl looks him up and down. Then spits at his feet.

"Nice kicking, dill weed." Before he can respond, she pivots and marches away.

Gonzalez watches her disappear down the pier.

Two weeks ago, the Dolphins held a Drake Maye-led Patriots offense to 3 points in the first half. Last week, that same defense limited Detroit's high-powered offense to one of its lowest point totals of the season. And while the final score on Sunday will show the Colts scored 20 points, the reality is a little different. After halftime, Indianapolis managed exactly three offensive points. Daniel Jones finished with fewer than 110 passing yards. The Dolphins intercepted him twice, returned one for a touchdown, forced a fumble and repeatedly forced Indianapolis off the field with three-and-outs. By the fourth quarter, the defense was dragging the rest of the team back into the game whether it wanted to come along or not.

The usual suspects were everywhere. Chris Johnson (59-yard pick six) continues to look like one of the steals of the draft. Michael Taaffe (6 tackles, 1 pass defended) once again found ways to impact the game. Chop Robinson (1 sack, 2 QB hits) consistently disrupted the pocket. Jordyn Brooks (9 tackles, 1 pass defended) was all over the field.

The Dolphins spotted Indianapolis seven points, generated almost nothing in the kicking game, and still found themselves with a chance to win in the final minutes because the defense spent the second half strangling the Colts offense. For a unit that has carried this team for much of the season, it was another outstanding performance.

Remember this scene from the greatest movie of all time?

The Dolphins' defense is now the Bluesmobile. The Dolphins entered the game without Zach Sieler. Then Jordan Phillips got hurt, and is out for the year. Then Zeek Biggers got hurt, and he's out for the year. By the end of the afternoon, Miami was essentially down to Kenneth Grant and Keith Cooper as healthy defensive tackles.

In-game, that degree of attrition eventually catches up with you. Without those defensive tackles, the run defense clearly felt the strain. Indianapolis finished with 172 rushing yards as Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan consistently found running lanes. The Dolphins simply didn't have their usual flexibility up front – too many snaps played by too few healthy bodies.

Miami's defense was good enough to win Sunday, but it wasn't healthy enough to win Sunday.

Let's get the obvious part out of the way first: Kyle McCord made mistakes. The strip-sack touchdown changed the game. The late sack in the fourth quarter was costly. Neither play can simply be ignored because he's a rookie.

But: The strip-sack wasn't the result of panic – it was a quarterback trying to make the correct read and reacting a second too slowly. The late sack wasn't a quarterback seeing ghosts as much as a young passer processing pressure incorrectly while trying to work deeper into the progression.

And then there's everything else. McCord converted a third-and-13. He made several NFL-caliber throws. He stayed aggressive. And he didn't fall apart after the strip-sack touchdown put seven points on the board for Indianapolis.

Young quarterbacks have gotten rattled by far less. Instead, McCord kept battling and gave Miami a chance to win. If you're looking for reasons to be optimistic, Sunday's mistakes looked fixable.

Back in August, I was so young and naïve, blinded by optimism that 2026 would lead to a glorious 6-11 season. Sure, we're rebuilding, but at least as the youngest team in the league, we would avoid some of those devastating injuries the league's more geriatric squads had to deal with.

Now? Now we have Kyle McCord handing the ball off to Ollie Gordon behind a leakier-than-expected offensive line. Our defensive tackles are so decimated, that we're down to three starters – Kenneth Grant, Keith Cooper and you, dear reader. Go suit up.

The team is still in evaluation mode, and there's still a lot of meaningful development that can and should happen for our first- and second-year starters. But the pipe dream of 6 wins feels especially unattainable now. At 38%, the Dolphins have the best odds to pick first in the 2027 draft, according to the prediction market platform Kalshi. ESPN gives the team a 41% chance, also first.

I'd like to see the Dolphins win against the Jets the Sunday after Thanksgiving. A two-win season isn't great, but if both wins come against the Jets, that can get me through the offseason.

#2785. Colts officially place Daniel Jones on waivers

Daniel Jones is officially on the waiver wire.

The NFL transaction report has gone out this afternoon, and Jones appears as a waiver from the Colts. After the trade deadline, every player who gets released by his team has to go on waivers before he becomes a free agent.

That means any team that wants Jones on his current contract can claim him, but that is extraordinarily unlikely to happen. As the waiver transaction notes, Jones is a vested veteran with a fully guaranteed salary for the rest of this season. No team is going to want to claim that salary.

Once he clears waivers, however, he’ll be an unrestricted free agent, free to sign with any team, and it won’t be surprising if some team wants to add him for veteran depth. Jones has been terrible this season, but he’s been a competent starter at times in his career, and a team that wants an experienced backup may be interested in signing him for a minimal salary.

Jones was also waived almost exactly two years ago, on November 22, 2024. He cleared waivers and signed with the Vikings’ practice squad before signing with the Colts after that season.

#2782. How Jacoby Brissett and Bryce Young compare ahead of Week 11 matchup

Jacoby Brissett goes to Carolina for his second Baltimore Ravens start with the same problem he faced in his first. The Ravens need to get Derrick Henry going early enough to keep the offense out of obvious passing situations. Bryce Young had that help from Chuba Hubbard in Carolina's win at New Orleans. This week, Young could have fewer options over the middle with tight ends Tommy Tremble and Darren Waller both listed as questionable, while Brissett already knows he can turn to Mark Andrews when the pocket closes.

Jacoby Brissett threw for 340 yards in his first start for the Baltimore Ravens. Bryce Young threw for 200 in Carolina's win at New Orleans. Both offenses finished with 20 points, and neither quarterback threw a touchdown pass. The difference was how they got there. Baltimore leaned on Brissett after its running game stalled. Carolina got 172 yards from scrimmage from Chuba Hubbard and a winning field goal as time expired.

Brissett completed 33 of 49 passes with one interception in a 23-20 loss. He took two sacks for nine yards, and Baltimore opened with three straight three-and-outs. The Ravens gained 16 rushing yards, though Derrick Henry scored both touchdowns on short runs. On the second touchdown drive, Brissett found Mark Andrews for 13 yards to the Los Angeles 4 before Henry finished the series. Andrews caught all eight of his targets for a team-high 82 yards.

Young went 17 of 30 for 200 yards with no interceptions and took three sacks for 14 yards. Tommy Tremble caught four passes for 48 yards and Darren Waller added two for 24. Their longest gains, 34 yards by Tremble and 13 by Waller, came on the same drive before Hubbard's first touchdown. On Carolina's winning possession, a pass interference penalty on a throw intended for Jalen Coker moved the ball 30 yards and set up Ryan Fitzgerald's 54-yard field goal.

Brissett had seven starts Arizona and one for Baltimore. Young has started all nine games for Carolina. The tight end matchup could look different Sunday because Carolina listed both Tremble and Waller as questionable with knee injuries. Andrews is already a reliable target for Brissett. If Young loses either of his tight ends, Hubbard's role as a receiver becomes even more important.
