#2776. Eye of the Tiger: Pivotal position matchups for LSU vs. Tennessee

Although the College Football Playoff wishes have sailed for LSU, there's still very much at stake in this game. Sitting at #9 with an 8-2 record, Tennessee is in a great spot to make the 12-team playoff for the second time under Josh Huepel. Each of their losses were by just a field goal. The first came at the end of September to then #1 Texas, then on the road at South Carolina. They have won 5 of their last 6, which is impressive considering they made a quarterback change 5 weeks ago.

The Volunteers entered 2026 with a massive question mark at the QB position. They felt strongly about last year's starter, Joey Aguilar, being able to get another year of eligibility, but he didn't. They then turned their attention to none other than…Sam Leavitt. We know how that story went, though. Lane Kiffin flew to Knoxville to meet Leavitt in the airport and convince him to commit to LSU and the rest is history.

True freshman Faizon Brandon started the first 5 games of the season for Tennessee, but it was never pretty. So, Huepel turned to redshirt freshman George MacIntyre and he's gone 4-1 as the starter.

LSU heads to Tennessee with a disappointing 6-4 record after a crushing collapse at home against Texas last week. Their season is effectively over and they are playing for pride for these final two regular season games.

We'll get our first peek at what Lane Kiffin's coaching looks like when things are going poorly. Will the Tigers come out fired up and looking to play spoiler? Or will they cower and lose their third straight?

We'll find out starting at 2:30 pm on Saturday in Neyland Stadium and here are three key matchups to look out for:

This one is pretty broad, but things are at an all time low for Leavitt. He was criticized heavily in the media for leaving the field prior to the alma mater as the team's leader, there were anti-Leavitt chants by students as they exited the stadium, and when given the ability to clear the air about some of when speaking publicly on Monday, he avoided it.

Now, he heads to Knoxville, the place he left high and dry to come back down to Baton Rouge. The Tennessee defense is ranked 3rd in total defense, 1st in scoring defense, and 1st against the pass. They sack the quarterback as much as anyone in the conference other than LSU, sitting just one short of the Tigers. It's a tough matchup, in a tough environment, in a tough time for Leavitt.

LSU offensive line vs. Tennessee defensive line

As I just mentioned, the Volunteers can get after the quarterback. They've racked up 39 sacks in 10 games. While 7 of those did come from Tyree Weathersby Sr, who is out for the season, they have plenty of other dudes that can get it done.

Xavier Gilliam and Mariyon Dye have 6 and 5 sacks, respectively, on the defensive line. Although he's listed as a linebacker, Arion Carter can come off of the edge and has 4 sacks of his own.Sam Leavitt was clearly hobbled last week against Texas. It looked to be his right leg/ankle, which is different from the left hamstring that he was successfully playing through earlier in the season. He looked hesitant to run and became scared to throw the ball after his third interception, putting his offensive line in a tough spot where they had to protect while he scrambled around in the backfield. That led to a few holding penalties when he exited the pocket before they expected him to.

Where this somehow gets even more concerning is when LSU tries to run the ball. As good as Dilin Jones is, he's had to make a lot of his magic on his own by making defenders miss. With Leavitt potentially compromised and the Tigers being in a hostile environment, they badly need to find a rushing attack to keep the Jim Knowles defense honest.

Blake Baker's run defense has been excellent all season. Despite missing Whit Weeks since week 4, they've been able to limit opposing running backs on a consistent basis. They've mostly been able to limit opposing offenses, in general, all season, but even when the other team has been able to move the ball, it's typically not on the ground. They're ranked #2 in the SEC in rush defense, allowing just 86.1 yards per game. Opponents are averaging just 2.73 yards per carry.

This week presents a true challenge, though. Allow me to introduce you to DeSean Bishop, the SEC's leading rusher. Wearing #18 for the Volunteers, Bishop has rushed for 1,163 yards with 13 touchdowns. He's averaging 5.1 yards per carry and has very seldom been slowed down. The only team that has limited him was Texas, who held him to 34 yards rushing in week 4.

Bishop has surpassed the century mark in rushing yards in 6 out of 10 games this season. In 2 of the games that he didn't, he finished with 97 yards. The only outliers are that game against Texas and their week 3 game against Kennesaw State, in which he had 9 carries for 42 yards and a touchdown before they took him out of the blowout and let then backup Daune Morris run for 116 yards.

The bottom line is, Tennessee can run the ball. Their offensive line is playing like one of the best in the country. They've only thrown the ball for over 200 yards twice the entire season. Brandon did it in the season opener against Furman and MacIntyre did it in his first start at Arkansas. Aside from that, the Volunteers have gotten to 8-2 and #9 in the country by running Bishop and playing defense.

Juventus are once again facing questions over their attacking recruitment, with Randal Kolo Muani struggling to justify the investment that brought him to Turin last summer. According to Gazzetta dello Sport, his future at the Allianz Stadium is already hanging by a thread.

Vlahovic endured an inconsistent spell towards the end of his Juventus career, but his goalscoring numbers still offered a level of productivity that Kolo Muani has struggled to replicate. The Frenchman has also failed to consistently influence games through his movement, link-up play, and ability to create opportunities for teammates.

Luciano Spalletti now faces the challenge of getting more out of an attacking department that has struggled to deliver consistently. Juventus have already seen their investment in center-forwards come under scrutiny, with the lack of goals placing additional pressure on the rest of the squad.

Unless Kolo Muani rediscovers his scoring touch, questions over Juventus' decision to prioritise him over Vlahovic are unlikely to disappear anytime soon. Furthermore, there's a chance he could leave Turin already at the end of this season.

#2773. Harden passes Bryant for 50-point games

James Harden scored 51 points to move third on the all-time list for 50-point NBA games as the Cleveland Cavaliers beat the Indiana Pacers 128-119 in the NBA Cup.

The 37-year-old made all 14 of his free throws as his recorded his 26th 50-point game to move above the legendary Kobe Bryant.

Harden, who also made six rebounds and provided six assists at Rocket Arena in Cleveland, had not passed 50 points since scoring 55 for the Los Angeles Clippers in November 2025.

Legendary centre Wilt Chamberlain holds the NBA record ⁠with 118 50-point games, while Michael Jordan is second with 31.

"When you talk about just basketball, obviously Wilt was elite, but you got Mike and Kobe - shooting guard position, the best to ever do it - so just to be in that conversation, it's very humbling and it's definitely special," said an emotional Harden.

Aged 37 years and 86 days, he is the fourth oldest player to score 50 points in a game.

"What excites me a lot is even being in my 18th year learning how to still be impactful," said Harden, the ninth highest scorer in NBA history with 29,633 points.

"It's easy when you're young - 23, 24, you run around, you jump high and can move fast and get by. Now it's like, you're not as fast.

"That's the evolution of James Harden and figuring that out.

"Tonight was a confidence-booster that I can do it at a high level still."

The Cavaliers travel to the Chicago Bulls in the NBA on Tuesday.

#2768. Nicolas Cage on his John Madden misfire: "I'm not Frank Caliendo"

This whole thing is antithetical to my identity.

That’s the one line that resonates most strongly in the new Madden movie. Because it’s exactly what John Madden would say if he saw it.

It’s bad. It’s very bad. Anyone who says it’s good has no taste and/or an agenda that involves the strategic application of lips to asses.

The biggest problem is Nicolas Cage as John Madden. Anyone who vividly remembers the unique charisma of John Madden knows instantly that nothing about Cage’s portrayal reflects the true nature, spirit, and demeanor of one of the most important and impactful figures in the entire history of the sport of football.

Cage, who seems to realize that his portrayal missed not only the bull’s-eye but also the entire wall on which the dart board was mounted, has defended the outcome by peering down his nose at the sports world.

“He was not on my radar,” Cage said of Madden, via Kirsten Chuba of the Hollywood Reporter. “I was growing up watching black-and-white Orson Welles movies and Fellini movies and Bruce Lee. I wasn’t interested in team sports whatsoever.”

“I’m someone that likes to stay out of his comfort zone and take a risk, I said yes, because that would be a transformation,” Cage explained regarding the decision to attempt to play the towering, iconic figure. “It would be something where I might learn a few things, taking on this character who is really nothing like me.”

The audience has learned that Cage’s interpretation is nothing like Madden.

“That’s what acting’s about,” Cage said. “I’m not an impressionist, I’m not Frank Caliendo. I lean more towards being a surrealist, meaning I like to get a concept of a personality and then dig deep and see what I can locate emotionally with my imagination and my psyche and filter it through the cadence and the appearance, within reason, of John Madden. I’m trying to give you an evocation, more or less, or an interpretation.”

The problem was it wasn’t even “within reason.” It was without reason. And the entire film was beyond unreasonable.

And I like Nicolas Cage. He was brilliant in Moonstruck. He won an Oscar for Leaving Las Vegas. And The Family Man remains a highly underrated holiday film.

Still, to quote another holiday film, “They can’t all be winners.” Cage’s role in Madden as John Madden is not.

I only met John Madden once. I watched him on TV for decades. I’ve heard plenty of stories about him from people who worked with him at NBC. And I’m confident that he would be livid about this film.

“That’s not me,” he’d say. “Not even close.”

Or, perhaps, “This whole thing is antithetical to my identity.”

#2766. Looking at Paul George’s torrid start shooting the 3

It's true that in the Boston Celtics' most recent defeat, a road loss to the Denver Nuggets, Paul George couldn't hit water if he fell out of a boat. Boston's second-leading scorer so far in the fledgling stages of the season misfired on all but one of his seven long-range tries, even throwing up an airball after a reload off an offensive board.

The 1-for-7 shooting night from deep was far from the only blemish on George's body of work Wednesday, too. He fouled out of a game for the first time as a Celtic, and foul trouble limited him to just 23 minutes played. But for as much as the nine-time All-Star had an off night, his cold shooting performance stands out as an outlier rather than a point of concern. After all, the numbers tell a story that suggests George's 3-point effectiveness so far in his maiden campaign in Boston has been almost unprecedented for a player of his age.

A fitting place to start when talking about George's long-range shooting chops this season is that he's spearheaded the Celtics' 3-point-heavy offensive attack. As has been the status quo under head coach Joe Mazzulla, the 3-point shot is once again a linchpin to Boston's modus operandi on that side of the ball, and no single Celtic has reaped the rewards of that style of play quite like George. On a team that employs plenty of elite 3-point marksmen such as Jayson Tatum, Payton Pritchard and Sam Hauser, it's impressively the veteran who paces the Celtics in 3s made per contest at 3.4.

The team-high 3.4 3s George is knocking down on a nightly basis is an especially impressive number when comparing that mark to players in their age-36 seasons. The list of players who have averaged three-plus converted triples per game at such a late stage in their NBA careers is microscopically small. Only Stephen Curry and James Harden have accomplished such a feat, and they're two of the greatest long-range snipers the game has ever seen. They're No. 1 and No. 2 on the league's all-time made 3s list, for reference.

Now, George's high-volume scoring from deep thus far would only be so valuable if the efficiency wasn't there, but he's blended volume and accuracy beautifully to this point. He's not only taking a lot of threes, but he's also finding nylon on a sizable chunk of those attempts. The California native has connected on well over 40 percent of his already 104 3s attempted — 42.3 percent to be exact, a career-high. Moreover, he ranks in the top ten among all qualified players in made 3s this season with 44, ahead of esteemed shooters such as Curry, Jalen Brunson, Donovan Mitchell, Tyrese Maxey and Kyrie Irving.

The fountain of youth is apparently located in Boston, as he is shooting the 3-ball at such a high level that Celtics fans have spent much of the season rubbing their eyes, wondering if they're watching the George of yesteryear who could go off for 30 on any given night. Highlighting his 3-point prowess alone might be unfair considering all the other things he's done well for the Celtics this season (defend off the ball, rebound, function as a secondary playmaker), but it's perhaps where he's made the biggest positive impact, and hopefully he can sustain the red-hot shooting.

#2761. NBA team grades: Report card for all 30 teams after the first month

The first month of the 2026-27 NBA season is in the books, and it's time to take stock of what's happened so far. Let's hand out some early grades.

It might be too soon to draw sweeping conclusions, but there's been enough basketball played to make preliminary judgements about the contenders falling short of expectations and the surprising teams surpassing what most experts anticipated. Evaluating each team's performance goes beyond its record, with roster construction, player development and overall trajectory factoring into whether a season is trending in the right direction.

Injuries to several stars and key contributors have shaped the league conversation through the opening month. Some teams have responded well to the adversity. Others have already dug themselves a hole that could prove difficult to escape. As a result, the grades cover a wide range of outcomes: six teams earned an A from USA TODAY Sports through the season's first month, while 10 received a D or F.

Here are grades for all 30 NBA teams now that the first month of the 2026-27 season is complete.

NBA PANIC METER: Which teams should worry after first month of season?

Records as of games played on Nov. 20. Preseason record projections via USA TODAY Sports.

The Hawks are right in the thick of the Eastern Conference playoff race again with guard Nickeil Alexander-Walker leading their backcourt, but there have been some troubling early signs. Jalen Johnson's production has dipped across the board from last season's breakout campaign, veteran closer C.J. McCollum is sidelined for at least another month and Atlanta has benefited from the NBA's second-easiest schedule to date. The Hawks' issues are flying under-the-radar, but they've struggled to show they belong among the East's top contenders when facing the NBA's best teams thus far.

After thriving without Jayson Tatum during much of last year's regular season, the Celtics haven't missed a beat in their first games since trading Jaylen Brown this past offseason. Tatum has elevated his playmaking, and Paul George looks rejuvenated as his new running mate in Boston. The Celtics have the NBA's best NET rating as of Nov. 18 and even got the better of Brown in their first matchup against the Philadelphia 76ers.

The Nets' roster is a mess because they've used seven first-round draft picks the past two years and none has demonstrated franchise-player potential to this point. Their top three guards (Egor Demin, Nolan Traore and Mikel Brown Jr.) haven't played much together yet due to minutes restrictions and skillset overlap. Their past four losses have come by an average of 24.5 points, and Julius Randle was spotted yelling at his teammates on the bench before calling their Nov. 18 loss to the Chicago Bulls "one of the worst games I've been a part of." After years of stockpiling assets, the Nets' rebuild still doesn't appear to have a clear path forward.

The Hornets perhaps expected to take a step back after trading LaMelo Ball this past offseason, but their start has muted much of the momentum generated from last year's encouraging run to the playoffs. Kon Knueppel lasted just nine minutes in his season debut before suffering a hamstring injury, and he's one of several key players to have missed games due to injury. The team, meanwhile, has the worst offensive rating in the league after finishing with the NBA's fifth-most efficient offense last season. Brandon Miller is shooting less than 35% from the field as the top offensive option, and Naz Reid, the primary acquisition in the Ball deal, was benched four games into the season by Hornets coach Charles Lee for "not meeting Hornets' standards." Just one month into the season, nearly everything that could have gone wrong for Charlotte has.

The Bulls are starting to emerge from a 1-9 start to the season, though their recent surge is happening right as No. 3 overall pick Caleb Wilson was diagnosed with a broken hand that will keep him out for the next few months. Wilson showed intriguing flashes in his early appearances, but it's still unclear whether Chicago's core featuring Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis is viable long-term. The Bulls feel closer to escaping the bottom-half of the Eastern Conference than they have been because of Wilson, but his injury means they'll have to wait longer to figure out exactly what they have.

The Cavaliers are off to a rougher-than-expected start to the season, and it's particularly concerning because their starters are the reason they're scuffling along. James Harden is showing his age more regularly, struggling to finish at the rim and get to the free throw line. Evan Mobley has already suffered a toe injury. Peyton Watson, the team's main offseason acquisition, looked completely out of sync before missing action recently with a back injury. Rookie Meleek Thomas and forward Mario Hezonja have been bright spots off the bench, but Cleveland's core has failed to resemble the group that reached the Eastern Conference finals last season.

Cooper Flagg appears to have taken another step forward in his development after winning Rookie of the Year, and his fit alongside Kyrie Irving has been better than many expected under new coach Dusty May. They've positioned the Mavericks as a legitimate play-in contender despite playing one of the tougher schedules in the league through 15 games. Their early success together strengthens the case for Irving to remain in Dallas beyond the NBA trade deadline. With a first-year NBA coach and a 19-year-old franchise star, the Mavericks are outperforming expectations through the season's first month.

The Nuggets remain a threat in the Western Conference playoff race, but there are some early signs that Denver's reign as a legitimate title contender could be waning. Nikola Jokic's 3-point shot has largely disappeared from his repertoire, a development that began after he returned from a wrist injury last season. His points, rebounds and assists per game have decreased compared to recent years. Jamal Murray's strong play has been offset by relatively uninspiring starts for veterans Aaron Gordon and DeMar DeRozan. It's no coincidence the team has gone from first in the league in offensive rating last year to 10th as of Nov. 19. If Jokic can't return to his MVP form and cover some of the roster flaws like he so often has over the past five years, it's hard to envision this group being a championship contender.

The Pistons were a trendy regression candidate in the East, but they've already got wins over the Boston Celtics, Miami Heat, Philadelphia 76ers and San Antonio Spurs through the first month of the season. Cade Cunningham is back in the MVP conversation, and Ausar Thompson is becoming one of the league's most disruptive two-way playmakers. Early injuries to Jalen Duren and offseason addition Isaiah Joe have taken a little shine off Detroit's strong start, but guard Daniss Jenkins is beginning to blossom into the secondary perimeter scoring option Cunningham has lacked in previous seasons.

The Warriors got an unexpected gift when rookie Yaxel Lendeborg quickly emerged as the leading NBA Rookie of the Year candidate and helped solve the team's void on the wing with Jimmy Butler sidelined. They reeled off eight-straight wins with Lendeborg serving as Steph Curry's sidekick. But Golden State dropped five games in a row after Curry suffered an oblique injury on Nov. 11, a development that has exposed Draymond Green's limitations and the lack of offense creation on the roster beyond Curry. Even so, Curry's eventual return and the prospect of Butler coming back gives Golden State more intrigue and upside than most expected entering the season.

The Rockets have looked like NBA title contenders through the season's first month, with the return of point guard Fred Van Vleet helping jump start the league's second-most efficient offense. Houston's turnovers are way down and its 3-point shooting is among the best in the NBA at the moment. Alperen Sengun, meanwhile, is on pace to break his career highs in points and assists as part of the Rockets' deep front court, and Kevin Durant remains one of the NBA's elite scorers. This appears to be one of the NBA's most complete rosters, blending ascending young talent with veterans who have extensive playoff experience. Considering the Rockets also possess the assets to make another significant move before the trade deadline, they may be San Antonio's biggest threat in the Western Conference.

The Pacers were hoping to rebound from last season's injury-induced tank, but they lost star Tyrese Haliburton to a hamstring injury after just four games. Indiana is one of the worst shooting teams in the league after one month, and it's wasting another strong start from Pascal Siakam. The lack of shooting has complicated Ivica Zubac's transition to the lineup, with poor spacing creating fit issues for a player Indiana spent considerable assets to acquire. He's on pace for his worst statistical season in six years. The Pacers entered the season expecting to rejoin the Eastern Conference contender tier, but they look much closer to a lottery team than a playoff threat right now.

The Clippers are in rebuilding mode and off to an uneven start, with the expectation they could be sellers at the trade deadline. The good news is that Darius Garland, the centerpiece of last year's James Harden trade, appears to have rediscovered his All-Star form after an injury-riddled 2025-26 season. The development of first-round pick Keaton Wagler alongside Garland is likely more important than the results the rest of the way, and he's shooting better than 40% from 3-point range since Nov. 2. The Clippers are one of the league's better shooting teams overall, but they've offset that strength by ranking among the NBA's most turnover-prone teams. They're likely headed for the lottery, but that's exactly where most anticipated them to be.

The Lakers are off to a fantastic start with Luka Dončić a leading MVP candidate and on pace to surpass Michael Jordan for the highest scoring average (38.1) since the 1976 NBA/ABA merger. Walker Kessler is also providing the dominating interior presence Los Angeles hoped for when it traded for him this offseason and gave him a huge contract. Kessler is averaging a double-double, while Austin Reaves is scoring more efficiently than at any point in his career. If Dončić continues to play at this level, the Lakers will be in the NBA title discussion come playoff time.

NBA MVP RANKINGS: There's a new No. 1, as Luka Dončić cedes ground

The Grizzlies have been the biggest surprise of the 2026-27 season thus far, vaulting toward the top of the Western Conference standings when many expected them to begin a rebuild after trading away Ja Morant, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Desmond Bane. Instead, the team's recent draft picks, particularly Cameron Boozer and Cedric Coward, have helped spearhead a balanced and remarkably deep roster that already looks like a playoff contender. A recent injury to veteran Ty Jerome looms large, but Cam Spencer has filled the void admirably thus far. Memphis owns the NBA's best offensive rating as of Nov. 20. Few saw that coming.

NBA observers were in panic mode when the Heat began the Giannis Antetokounmpo era with four losses in a row, but Miami is 9-2 since then with an increasingly potent offense built around pace and space. Antetokounmpo is leading the Heat with the fourth-highest scoring average in the NBA (28.2 points), and Davion Mitchell leads the NBA in assists per game. Only the Spurs' starters have a better NET rating than the Heat lineup featuring Antetokounmpo, Bam Adebayo, Klay Thompson, Mitchell and Pelle Larsson among groups that have played at least 65 minutes together. One month into the season, Miami appears to have already discovered the lineup it can trust most when playoff games are on the line.

The Bucks were expected to be bad this season after trading Giannis Antetokounmpo, but they're off to the worst start in franchise history with the league's worst record and own the worst NET rating in the Eastern Conference as of Nov. 20. With veterans like Myles Turner, Kyle Kuzma and Gary Trent Jr. taking up salary cap space after being acquired in prior seasons, this rebuild appears to only just be beginning. Milwaukee entered the post-Giannis era without a clear franchise cornerstone, and the first month of the season has done little to change that. It will be painful for Bucks' fans this season.

The Timberwolves have done a fine job keeping pace in the competitive Western Conference after losing Anthony Edwards to a knee injury that required arthoscopic surgery. LaMelo Ball, Ayo Dosunmu, Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert have formed a well-rounded core that could be dangerous if Edwards returns before the playoffs. There is no timetable on his recovery, though Edwards told reporters on Nov. 19 he is planning to to come back this season. Minnesota's ceiling ultimately depends on his health.

The Pelicans got off to a bad start, won four games in a row and now appear headed nowhere fast once again. Dejounte Murray's recent trade request brought renewed attention to one of the NBA's most confusing roster situations. New Orleans hasn't been able to win consistently despite Zion Williamson enjoying one of the healthiest stretches of his career, and Trey Murphy III is increasingly viewed as one of the league's more attractive trade targets. Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen are intriguing young players, but both have contributed to the defensive issues that have left New Orleans among the NBA's worst teams on that end of the floor. Murray, meanwhile, is owed enough money that moving him won't be simple. If this start continues, Joe Dumars would have to consider a roster overhaul.

The Knicks deserve the benefit of the doubt after a sluggish start coming off an NBA championship, though the early-season struggles of Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges, as well as the ongoing contract situation involving Karl-Anthony Towns, bear watching. Jalen Brunson and Towns continue to form one of the NBA's most potent duos, and New York remains firmly positioned in the Eastern Conference playoff picture thanks in large part to one of the league's best defenses. The Knicks proved last season they can reach another level when the games matter most.

The Thunder are doing their best to stay afloat in the crowded Western Conference standings playing without Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren and Cason Wallace due to injuries. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander remains one of the league's best players, and OKC's deep reservoir of first-round picks is paying off with younger players like Ajay Mitchell and rookie Aday Mara successfully stepping into larger roles. The Thunder have survived a difficult opening month and came out looking capable of remaining in the playoff mix. But bad injury luck could prevent them from contending for a title this season.

The Magic hoped to emerge as Eastern Conference contenders, but they finished the opening month of the season below .500 and lost star Paolo Banchero to injury after just two games. A recent four-game winning streak that included a victory over the Boston Celtics showcased the potential of a group built around Franz Wagner, Desmond Bane, Anthony Black and a healthy Jalen Suggs. But the franchise is still no closer to determining whether Banchero and Wagner can thrive together as a long-term foundation. Until Banchero returns, that question will remain unanswered, and Orlando appears destined to be part of the crowded pack of Eastern Conference teams battling to avoid the play-in tournament.

After considerable preseason hype and past stumbles out of the gate for LeBron James-led superteams, the Sixers finished the first month of the 2026-27 season tied with the Spurs for the NBA's best record. James and Jaylen Brown have blended in well with Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid and VJ Edgecombe, though the team's starting lineup had a surprising -4.9 NET rating playing together through 16 games. It speaks to some of the unexpected depth Philadelphia enjoys, with Dean Wade, Anfernee Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope forming a versatile rotation. One month into the season, the 76ers look like the team to beat in the Eastern Conference.

The Suns have rebounded from a rough start to the season despite playing one of the toughest schedules in the league, and Devin Booker remains among the NBA's top 12 scorers. But their two most-used lineups have been outscored by an average net rating of 15.5 points per 100 possessions. Jalen Green is having the least productive season of his career, and centers Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Maluach have looked overmatched while replacing the injured Mark Williams. As currently constructed, Phoenix looks capable of reaching the play-in tournament. But unless the Suns can find an upgrade before the trade deadline, their ceiling appears to be a first-round playoff exit.

The Trail Blazers have taken a step forward with wins over the Lakers and Thunder already. Damian Lillard is providing a perimeter scoring punch, and his presence hasn't come at the expense of Deni Avdija. It's turned a lackluster offense into one with a top-10 NET rating thus far. It remains to be seen how Ja Morant's return from a hamstring injury affects the rotation, but early returns suggest Portland's crowded backcourt can co-exist. This might not be a legitimate title contender, but the Trail Blazers look as feisty as they have at any point since Lillard led them to the Western Conference Finals in 2019.

The Kings appear to be the most dysfunctional team in the league, with a core of expensive veteran players who don't seem interested in remaining in Sacramento but lack significant trade value. Rookie Darius Acuff Jr. has been a bright spot, on pace to average the most points by a first-year player since Michael Jordan. But the Kings haven't translated that production into wins and they have the league's worst NET rating. Meanwhile, last year's breakout rookie, 23-year-old center Maxime Raynaud, has yet to play due to injury. This directionless franchise is no closer to finding its way.

The Spurs have looked every bit like a team on a mission to avenge last June's NBA Finals loss, highlighted by a recent 12-game winning streak. Victor Wembanyama is an MVP candidate once again, and the returning core of Dylan Harper, Stephon Castle and De'Aaron Fox has made the absence of free-agent acquisition Tobias Harris largely an afterthought. A recent hip injury to Harper does not appear to be serious, and San Antonio is deep enough to withstand his absence if he misses additional time. One month into the season, the Spurs look like the favorites to win the NBA title.

After emerging as one of the NBA's pleasant surprises last season, the Raptors have stumbled out of the gate this year. Kawhi Leonard has yet to play because of a knee injury, and Scottie Barnes has also missed time. The team's defense has gone from a strength to a weakness, particularly in close games, and Toronto ranks among the NBA's worst rebounding teams because of a wing-heavy roster that lacks a reliable center. The Raptors traded for Leonard with championship aspirations in mind, but the first month of that pursuit has been anything but encouraging.

The Jazz's hopes of emerging as a playoff contender after a lengthy rebuilding have been decimated by injuries to Lauri Markannen and Jaren Jackson Jr., as well as a disastrous start that featured a 12-game losing streak. Keyonte George played more like a rising star in two recent Utah wins and, along with rookie Darryn Peterson and 20-year-old Ace Bailey, gives the franchise a promising young core. But the Jazz expected to compete for a postseason berth and that might not be possible after an opening month that could hardly have gone worse.

The Wizards remain near the bottom of the Eastern Conference standings, and their decision to give Trae Young a $212 million contract extension is already drawing scrutiny. Young is shooting a career-worst 30.4% from 3-point range, and Washington ranks as the NBA's second-worst 3-point shooting team. Opponents have also targeted Young defensively in crunch time. The team's struggles are particularly concerning because Anthony Davis is healthy and playing well, while rookie AJ Dybantsa has shown encouraging flashes despite struggling to shoot from outside since returning from injury. Washington may still have enough talent to reach the playoffs in the East, but its biggest investment is underperforming.

#2759. Packers should lean on running back Kaleb Johnson after their bye

The bright spots of the Packers' Week 10 loss to the Vikings are few and far between, but running back Kaleb Johnson was surely among them.

"I thought he did a nice job," LaFleur said of Johnson's 10-carry, 42-yard outing. "I liked how he was hitting the hole, running with good pad level, pressing the line of scrimmage. I thought that was a positive performance."

If there's a big takeaway to be had here, it's that Johnson should be getting the lion's share of carries going forward, and probably deserves more snaps, too.

Josh Jacobs remains a mystery. He's on track to return in relatively short order from finger surgery, but a potential suspension still looms like the sword of Damocles. He wasn't overly effective as a runner in his brief return to the lineup, either. Across three games, Jacobs carried 36 times for just 80 yards, an abysmal 2.2 yards per carry. Even the perpetually disappointing MarShawn Lloyd has managed 2.7 yards per attempt this year.

Speaking of Lloyd, even if he's better than Jacobs this year, he's obviously not the future or the present at the position. Kudos to him for making it all the way back from his various injury issues over the last couple of seasons, but it's abundantly clear he can't get the job done. It's hard to foresee him improving much even if the Packers make major strides on the offensive line.

Chris Brooks, meanwhile, is a solid but limited player. It's probably better to think of him as a fullback at this point, a latter day John Kuhn who mostly finds his way to the field because he's not going to screw it up for the Packers in pass protection.

And since Pierre Strong Jr. has now been released, that leaves us with Johnson as the last remaining back on the roster, and perhaps the most viable.

The big problem with Johnson to this point has been his limited value in the passing game. You can see what the Packers think of him there by just look at his snap usage. He was on the field for 13 snaps against the Vikings and carried the ball on 10 of them. As a rule, they don't want him catching passes or blocking for Jordan Love.

But LaFleur did call out Johnson's pass blocking as his most notable contribution on Sunday. Johnson stonewalled a blitzing linebacker on a 19-yard completion.

"The thing I was most pleased with was one of the protections when we hit [Tucker Kraft], he came across and picked up Eric Wilson on the blitz right in the B gap," LaFleur said.

You don't have to be a tape grinder to see what LaFleur is talking about. Johnson lines up to Jordan Love's left on the play, but alertly comes across the formation to pick off Wilson just as he jets past Travis Glover. Love completes the pass to Kraft, and the Packers would go on to score three points on the drive, cutting the Vikings' lead to just 10 points. In theory, it could have been a pivotal play.

The fact is that Johnson is the only back doing anything even close to making pivotal plays this season. The Packers have only had a back rush for 40 or more yards in a game three times this season, and Johnson is responsible for all three of those occurrences. The Packers will probably never have a good running game this season, but if they're going to do anything at all on the ground, it's probably going to be because Johnson is getting the work done.

#2758. Bud Dupree requests release from Chargers, who haven't granted it

As the season continues to unfold — and as the trade deadline fades into the rear-view mirror — unhappy players have only one option: To request a release.

Via Jeremy Fowler of ESPN, Chargers linebacker Bud Dupree has done that. The Chargers, however, have not granted the request.

Dupree, per Fowler, also requested his release before the season.

It’s unknown whether the Chargers tried to trade him. His playing time has systematically dropped this year. He had no defensive snaps in two straight games before he was a healthy scratch in the Week 10 Monday night game against the Ravens.

That move came three days after Dupree had some pointed comments for the front office.

“Don’t ask hard questions to us; ask hard questions to them,” Dupree said. “Ask the hard questions. Everybody pull they cameras out and go upstairs and ask questions to them. Everybody. Walk upstairs and ask them.”

Dupree is under contract, so there’s nothing he can do to force his way out. Still, the situation underscores the one-way nature of these deals.

The team can cut the player whenever it wants. The player can’t get out unless the team is willing to let him go.

#2756. NFL Week 11 best bets: Bills, Bears and Chiefs lay big home numbers

NFL Week 11 best bets run through 10 Sunday afternoon games, and the Chiefs' 16.5-point line against Arizona and a 37.5-point total in Philadelphia draw the biggest plays at 2.5 units each.

Each spread and total pick carries a unit rating from 0 to 3 units. Philadelphia sticks with quarterback Joe Milton through a seven-game losing streak, while Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur is preparing Josh Johnson to start with rookie Carson Beck questionable because of a back injury.

MORE: Week 11 fantasy football PPR rankings: Burrow tops QBs as Bowers injury looms

Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) warms up before the game against the Minnesota Vikings | Matt Krohn-Imagn Images

Picks: Bills 31-10, Bills -16.5 (2u), Under 44.5 (1u)

Buffalo (8-1) has won five straight under Bills coach Joe Brady, and Miami (1-8) arrives thin in the secondary. Cornerback Jaylin Simpson and safety Dante Trader Jr. are doubtful, per Friday's injury updates, so Bills quarterback Josh Allen should find open receivers downfield.

The Dolphins lost 24-22 at Indianapolis last week after kicker Zane Gonzalez missed two field goals and an extra point, and they've thrown only seven touchdown passes all season. Bills tight end Dalton Kincaid is doubtful, but Buffalo has enough elsewhere to score four touchdowns. One Miami touchdown keeps that finish under 44.5.

Picks: Bears 27-13, Bears -11.5 (1.5u), Under 48.5 (2u)

New Orleans (3-6) ruled out tackles Taliese Fuaga and Asim Richards along with center Erik McCoy, so its patched-up line faces a Chicago defense that helped carry the Bears to four straight wins. Saints linebacker Pete Werner is also questionable.

The Bears (7-2) come off their bye, and Bears quarterback Caleb Williams needs a cleaner game after four interceptions in a narrow win over Tampa Bay. Running back Kyle Monangai has no injury designation, so Chicago can lean on the run once it builds a lead. I like the under more than laying 11.5 because a late Saints touchdown could spoil the cover without threatening the total.

Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward (1) looks to pass during the second quarter against the Jacksonville Jaguars | Steve Roberts-Imagn Images

Picks: Cowboys 30-24, Titans +7.5 (2u), Under 54.5 (0.5u)

Titans quarterback Cam Ward has completed 54 of 79 passes for 535 yards, four touchdowns and one interception over his last two games, according to the Titans' preview. "The way we are trending is going upward," Ward said Wednesday.

Dallas ranks last in total defense, has allowed 1,541 rushing yards and gave up 46 points to San Francisco last week. The Cowboys also ruled out tight end Jake Ferguson, guard Tyler Booker, cornerback DaRon Bland and safety P.J. Locke. Dallas can still score against a one-win Titans team, but a six-point Cowboys win leaves Tennessee inside the number. Titans receiver Carnell Tate and running back Tyjae Spears are questionable.

MORE: Week 11 fantasy football QB start-sit: Goff, Nix, Purdy, Ward

Picks: Lions 23-19, Buccaneers +5.5 (1u), Under 45.5 (2u)

Detroit (7-2) has allowed just 14.4 points per game during its five-game winning streak, per the Buccaneers' game preview. Tampa Bay (3-6) can match that defensively after intercepting 5.21% of opposing passes, the highest rate in the league, though safety Antoine Winfield Jr. is out.

Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield is questionable with foot and thumb injuries. Buccaneers coach Todd Bowles said Friday that he's "trending in the right direction." Even with Mayfield, Tampa Bay has a league-low six touchdown passes, so Lions quarterback Jared Goff and Detroit should win a low-scoring game by less than a touchdown.

Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid looks on during the second quarter against the Indianapolis Colts | Jay Biggerstaff-Imagn Images

Picks: Chiefs 30-9, Chiefs -16.5 (2.5u), Under 40.5 (0.5u)

Kansas City (7-2) beat Atlanta 35-13 last week behind five touchdown passes from Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes. Arizona (3-7) has allowed 22 passing touchdowns, tied for the most in the league, and lost 34-6 to the Rams in Beck's first start, when he went 11 of 18 for 108 yards with two interceptions.

Beck or Johnson will face a Kansas City defense that has allowed only seven touchdown passes. Running back Kenneth Walker III and guard Trey Smith are out, but rookie Emmett Johnson ran for 101 yards and caught two touchdown passes against Atlanta. The under is the thinner play because a short field could push the Chiefs past 30.

Picks: Steelers 20-13, Steelers -3.5 (1.5u), Under 37.5 (2.5u)

Milton completed 18 of 34 passes for 169 yards and took seven sacks in a 19-11 loss to the Giants in his first start. He spent the bye learning the offense and summed up the change simply: "What's different? My confidence."

Pittsburgh (6-3) has allowed only 749 rushing yards and five rushing touchdowns, and Philadelphia owns the league's lowest offensive success rate. The Steelers rank 30th in pass defense, but Milton hasn't shown he can take advantage. Eagles receiver DeVonta Smith is cleared, while linebacker Zack Baun is out. Steelers receivers Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson are questionable. Two Steelers touchdowns and two field goals cover the spread and stay well under 37.5.

Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young (9) throws a pass against the Philadelphia Eagles | Eric Hartline-Imagn Images

Picks: Panthers 24-20, Panthers -3 (1u), Over 43.5 (0.5u)

Ravens quarterback Jacoby Brissett threw for 340 yards in his first Baltimore start, but the Ravens (4-6) ran for a season-low 16 yards in a 23-20 loss to the previously winless Chargers. Running back Derrick Henry had 10 yards on 10 carries as Baltimore dropped its fifth straight.

Cornerback Marlon Humphrey has been deactivated after the team sent him home Thursday over derogatory podcast comments, and defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike and safety Jaylinn Hawkins are also out. Carolina (4-5) beat New Orleans 20-17 last week, and Panthers quarterback Bryce Young should face less pressure against this depleted front. The Panthers have allowed 14 rushing touchdowns, so Henry should bounce back near the goal line and push this over.

MORE: Week 11 fantasy football WR start-sit: Allen, Mitchell, Tucker, Waddle

Picks: Jets 20-17, Jets +3 (1.5u), Under 42.5 (2u)

Jets quarterback Geno Smith is off the injury report after hurting his ankle against Buffalo. "He looks solid, he looks solid," Jets coach Aaron Glenn said Friday. "It's very encouraging."

Los Angeles (1-8) won for the first time at Baltimore, but Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert has been sacked 33 times, and the Chargers entered last week last in scoring. New York has the league's worst red-zone touchdown rate and won't have receivers Omar Cooper Jr. and Isaiah Williams, so field goals should keep this low even if the Jets win outright. Chargers receiver Ladd McConkey is questionable, and Brenen Thompson is doubtful.

MORE: Week 11 waiver wire FAAB: Michael Mayer, Ryan Flournoy top fantasy football adds

Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza (15) shakes hands with Seattle Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock (2) | Gary A. Vasquez-Imagn Images

Picks: Broncos 24-13, Broncos -10.5 (0.5u), Under 40.5 (1.5u)

Raiders rookie Fernando Mendoza makes his second start after going 11 of 13 for 90 yards with a rushing touchdown against Seattle, though he was sacked six times. Denver (7-2) has won five straight and sits tied for first in the AFC West.

Raiders coach Klint Kubiak faces his former team and said he's "looking forward to going back to the stadium and being a part of this game." Las Vegas (4-6) also has the league's worst run-blocking grade, so Mendoza could face plenty of third-and-longs. Denver's offense hasn't been explosive enough to trust at -10.5, which is why the under gets the bigger rating. Raiders tight end Brock Bowers and Broncos safety Brandon Jones are questionable.

Picks: Jaguars 24-20, Giants +6 (1.5u), Under 46.5 (1u)

Jacksonville (7-2) leads the NFL with a +125 point differential and beat Tennessee 40-23 last week as Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence threw for 352 yards and three touchdowns. Running back Bhayshul Tuten is off the injury report, while defensive end Danny Striggow is questionable.

The Giants (5-3-1) lost a fourth-quarter lead for the first time this season against Washington, but Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy set career highs with 23 completions and 293 passing yards. Giants coach John Harbaugh also has a defense that holds up against the pass, so New York can keep this within a touchdown at home.

#2754. Jaguars saw something in Liam Coen that other teams didn't

In a season and a half with the Jaguars, Liam Coen has established himself as one of the best coaches in the NFL. Last year, Coen took over a team that had gone 4-13 the year before and improved their record to 13-4 — the best record ever for a first-year coach taking over a team that had won four or fewer games the year before. This year Coen is showing that last year was no fluke, with the Jaguars at 7-2 with an NFL-best point differential of +125.

Coen’s great success should have other teams that hired new head coaches in 2025 asking themselves: What did we miss? Because the Jaguars were so high on Coen that he was their No. 1 target and they were willing to do whatever it took to get him, while no other team even bothered to give Coen an interview.

During the 2025 NFL coaching search, we tracked dozens of reports of head coaching interviews and requests among the seven teams that had vacancies. The Jaguars were the only team that so much as asked Coen to interview.

This week there’s been some media scrutiny on the Jets, who hired Aaron Glenn without considering Coen as a candidate. Glenn is 5-22; Coen is 20-6. But it’s unfair to single out the Jets for failing to interview Coen, because no team other than the Jaguars did, either.

The 41-year-old Coen had a résumé that should have made him a good candidate. NFL teams area always on the lookout for coaches who can nurture a franchise quarterback and run an innovative offense. Coen played quarterback at UMass and coached quarterbacks in college before getting hired by Sean McVay to work on the Rams’ staff, eventually became the Rams’ offensive coordinator under McVay, and had been a successful playcaller as offensive coordinator for the Buccaneers, as well as at Kentucky. With that background, it’s surprising that only the Jaguars wanted him.

And the Jaguars really wanted him, to the point that they were willing to do whatever it took to hire him. Coen initially turned the Jaguars down and agreed to a contract extension to stay with the Buccaneers, but Jaguars owner Shad Khan wouldn’t take no for an answer. When Coen said he was concerned about the direction of the Jaguars’ front office, Khan fired General Manager Trent Baalke and agreed to reshape the front office in a way that Coen would approve of if Coen would take the job. Coen was persuaded to take the Jaguars job, and the Jaguars later hired James Gladstone, who had worked with Coen on the Rams, as GM.

The result has been the Jaguars going from one of the worst teams in the NFL to one of the best. Coen’s success in Jacksonville has justified the faith Khan had in him. And raises questions about the total lack of interest from the rest of the league.

#2748. Philadelphia mayor wants the Eagles to play in a dome

The Eagles will become an indoor team if the mayor of Philadelphia gets her way.

“I want a dome,” Mayor Charelle L. Parker said on 93.3 WMMR, via the Philadelphia Inquirer. “Don’t you tell. This is a secret between us. I just saw a rendering of this beautiful dome that they’re talking about for the Bears.”

Moving into a dome would change the character of late-season and playoff games in Philadelphia, which are often affected by snow, wind and cold. Plenty of fans won’t like it. But politicians and NFL owners often prefer stadiums with roofs because they bring in lucrative events, indoor sports, concerts, conventions and trade shows.

The Eagles told season ticket holders last year that they are looking at either renovations to Lincoln Financial Field or a new stadium. Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie has committed only to staying in “the region,” not in the city of Philadelphia, but both Parker and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro have said they want the Eagles to remain in the city.

The Eagles’ lease at Lincoln Financial Field runs through the 2032 season.

#2744. Walker Kessler's first three-pointer as a Laker sparks resurgent second half

Lakers coaches didn't know why Walker Kessler was standing in the corner. But when Collin Sexton flung the ball to the center standing behind the three-point arc on the Lakers' first possession of the fourth quarter, Kessler knew what he was going to do with it.

"I'm confident in that shot," Kessler said with a smirk.

The 7-foot-2 center's strong second half sparked the Lakers' gritty 106-104 win over the Sacramento Kings on Friday at Crypto.com Arena. After Lakers coach JJ Redick "lit [him] up" at halftime, Kessler responded by scoring nine of his 15 points and grabbing six of his seven total rebounds after the break and draining the unexpected long-distance shot that put the Lakers up by one early in the fourth quarter.

Redick said the play, with the Lakers (14-3) trailing by two to start the fourth quarter, was a little unorganized, leading to their center somehow standing in the corner. Kessler, who hadn't attempted a three all season and was 17 for 64 from three-point range during four seasons with the Utah Jazz, took instruction from Sexton to space to the corner instead of slash to the rim. Sexton whipped a one-handed pass over his head to Kessler, who methodically rose up over Dylan Cardwell's late closeout.

Redick told Kessler once during the preseason after a particular timeout that if the ball found him on a called play and it wasn't for a layup, the center should still shoot. Although Kessler has faith from the coaches and works on his jump shot, Redick isn't anointing the 25-year-old an official stretch five. His teammates don't mind.

"I mean, if he shoots it like that, I'll keep finding him," guard Quentin Grimes said with a laugh. "If he's going to keep cashing it all net, I want more of them. Keep shooting."

Read more: Quentin Grimes' late three-pointer lifts Lakers to narrow win over Kings

Kessler's go-ahead three-pointer highlighted the Lakers' comeback from an 11-point deficit with 11:25 remaining in the third. During a homestand that appeared to be favorable but has turned into a difficult slog, the Lakers have relied on unexpected characters to star in big moments.

Grimes hit back-to-back three-pointers in the fourth quarter against the Charlotte Hornets on Tuesday to fuel his career-high 47 points. The Lakers staged most of their 18-point comeback during the beginning of the fourth quarter when superstar Luka Doncic was on the bench. They trailed by 13 at the end of the third quarter. When Doncic subbed back in with 6:54 remaining, the Lakers, playing the majority of the stretch with two-way center Carson Cooper, were down by only four.

Cooper was playing the critical minutes because Kessler missed the game with lower right leg soreness. With Kessler back against the Kings (1-14), the Lakers repeated their fourth-quarter heroics, turning a two-point deficit after three quarters into a seven-point lead by the time Doncic returned.

Coaches made small rotational changes to the unit Friday, opting to start the fourth with Kessler, Sexton, Grimes, Matisse Thybulle and Jake LaRavia. Forward Sandro Mamukelashvili previously started the fourth quarter in recent games with Austin Reaves sidelined. Still feeling out the best lineups for the team, Redick said the exact groupings are "going to be a process."

The Lakers aren't fazed by the adjustments.

"I think we have a lot of heart and our ability to just make things work," said Thybulle, who had 14 points and four made three-pointers Friday. "We've been throwing out a whole bunch of different lineups. … Just being able to be adaptable, I think, has been a huge thing for everyone on the roster."

Lakers center Walker Kessler scores off an offensive rebound in the first half against the Sacramento Kings on Friday. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

The Lakers are 6-1 in the last seven games in which Doncic or Reaves have missed time. The superstars have only played three quarters of a game together in the last seven games. Doncic missed the game at Detroit with lower back soreness, and Reaves, who was sick in Atlanta on Nov. 9, has missed the last four games with a left heel bruise. The Lakers hope to have him back by at least next Friday on the road against San Antonio.

Kessler was sidelined against Charlotte for the first time this season. Like the rest of his teammates, he struggled against the Utah Jazz on Wednesday, finishing with the quietest 10-point, 11-rebound double-double imaginable. He was in danger of fading into the background again against Sacramento before Redick jolted the team awake at halftime.

"I wasn't playing physical," Kessler said. "I wasn't going up to dunk the ball. I was missing some more touches around the rim. And then defensively, being undisciplined. Jumping at stuff I don't need to jump at. He definitely lit into me. It was good. I needed it. That's what makes a good coach. Knowing when guys need that and when guys don't."

While Redick said afterward he believed he was able to regulate his emotions during his halftime talk to the team, Doncic, who finished with 25 points and eight assists, characterized it more plainly.

"He yells," Doncic said. "But I'm used to it."

Kessler, a center piece for a franchise with championship expectations, is getting used to the demands of this new spotlight. He dazzled with 48 points in his first two games in which he made 22 of 26 shots, including 10 dunks in his perfect debut. But coaches demanded more production from his rebounding and fans are unrelenting in their calls for more.

"I know obviously you're on a bigger stage and stuff like that, but my teammates and coaching staff have done a really good job of picking everyone up even though we're struggling or we were struggling these past two games," Kessler said. "I'm not really focused too much on the outside but I understand that the L.A. fans expect a certain kind of performance. And I think it's not just making shots, but playing with effort and energy and I can completely respect that."

When Kessler goes to the bench, he hears jeers from fans imploring him to play harder.

When he drained that three from the corner, he heard some of the loudest cheers of the night.

#2743. NFL didn't know Puka Nacua had surgery when agreeing to suspension

The sudden decision of the NFL to suspend receiver Puka Nacua three games raises plenty of relevant questions. On Friday, a technically irrelevant question was answered.

After Rams coach Sean McVay disclosed to reporters that Nacua had surgery to repair a torn MCL suffered during a Week 9 win over the Commanders, Judy Battista of NFL Network reported this: “The NFL did not know Puka Nacua had had knee surgery on Tuesday when it suspended him yesterday.”

Surely, that’s accurate; Judy is a solid reporter. But that extra fact doesn’t matter to the NFL’s ultimate handling of Nacua.

The report creates the impression that, during the negotiations that resulted in the three-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy, Nacua and/or his representatives withheld material information. That, at some level, the league had been duped by the lack of knowledge that Nacua had undergone surgery that will sideline him for “a couple months.”

First, the suspension (as the league affirmatively explained on Thursday) is separate from the injury. The NFL listed multiple examples of players who served suspensions while injured.

Second, whether Nacua (who had already missed one of the four minimum games he’s required to miss while on IR), was already going to serve the entirety of the suspension while on injured reserve with or without surgery.

Third, the surgery and the extended absence actually avoids the possibility that Nacua would have returned to action exactly one game after finishing his suspension, resulting in no net games missed due to the suspension.

The mere existence of the report represents an implicit acknowledgement by the league that the negotiated suspension, aimed at allowing Nacua to double-dip when it comes to his stint on injured reserve and his suspension, underscores the broader question of whether players should be allowed to serve a suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy when otherwise unable to play. That’s a separate issue for the NFL to revisit, if it chooses, through a potential revision to the terms of the policy.

As explained on Friday, the league could have refused the deal. It could have insisted on pushing the issue through the full process, with Judge Sue L. Robinson conducting a hearing and the outcome potentially being appealed (by Nacua and/or the league) to the Commissioner. But that would have entailed a non-zero-percent chance that Nacua wouldn’t have been suspended at all.

For Nacua, the goal was to get the suspension served while injured. The fact that he had surgery before the agreement was reached gave him more of a buffer than the NFL knew about, expanding the window during which the suspension could be fully served before the end of the 2026 season without Nacua missing time due to the suspension. Which would still allow Nacua to have this issue behind him before the 2027 offseason, when he signs a new contract with the Rams, has the franchise tag applied, or becomes a free agent.

Of course, Nacua now needs to tread lightly. The league has made it clear that “any further violation of the Personal Conduct Policy, including failing to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program, will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the League.” To the extent that the league isn’t thrilled by the perception/reality that it allowed Nacua to serve his suspension at a time when he otherwise could not play, the league could be ready to pounce on any opportunity to impose a longer suspension that would apply when Nacua is healthy again.

And Portland just had a great offensive game against Milwaukee. Lillard scored 33 points, Scoot Henderson added 27, and Holiday finished with 22. That's 82 points from three guards, and they did it without Avdija. If those guys keep making shots, Portland can definitely make this a close game.

Clingan needs to stay out of foul trouble and stop Towns from getting too many rebounds. If he can do that, Portland should have a better chance.

I'm taking the Knicks in a close game. Portland has been better offensively, but New York has the stronger defense and should have an advantage on the boards. The Knicks rank second in points allowed and third in offensive rebounding rate, while Portland is sixth in scoring. Avdija being questionable is another big problem for the Blazers, and I think Brunson and Towns will do enough to get another win at home.

#2739. Raiders owner Mark Davis hated the Madden movie

The new Madden movie includes a brief, fleeting glance of a young Mark Davis. The depiction wasn’t flattering.

His assessment of the film is far less flattering.

The Raiders owner teed off on the Madden movie, in an interview with John Katsolimetes of the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

“My comment is, it’s full of turducken,” Davis said initially.

“It depends on whether you like turducken or not, and obviously, I don’t like turducken,” Davis said.

“I think it’s really it’s unfair to take people that have passed away and make caricatures out of them, and try to sell it as truth,” Davis said. “They start the movie with a statement saying that all of it’s not true, but some of it is, so it’s confusing what to believe.”

That’s not an uncommon device. “Based on a true story” means that plenty of liberties will be taken in an effort to make the story more compelling.

Mark Davis had one specific concern regarding the shading of the truth. He objected to his father’s reaction to the serious neck injury suffered by Patriots receiver Darryl Stingley, during a preseason game in 1978.

“So John goes over to the hospital afterwards, you know, and really looks after him,” Mark Davis said, “and there’s a scene where my dad is telling John, ‘You don’t need to go over there. You don’t need to take care of other teams’ players. You take care of our players.’

“That’s just so far from the truth. Anybody who has ever known him knows my dad always took care of people behind the scenes. If it was a player from another team had an issue that wasn’t being taken care of, my dad would quietly take care of that even if it was players on other teams. I’m serious. . . . It just it felt cheap to me to build up John’s image at the expense of my father’s.”

Davis praised Christian Bale for his portrayal of Al Davis.

“You can’t blame the script on him,” Mark Davis said. “He tried.”

Mark Davis also didn’t care for the characterization of the iconic John Madden by Nicolas Cage.

“You know, he at times did look like John, but he wasn’t John,” Davis said. “I mean, they made John to be a pussy, and John was the farthest thing from a pussy.”

The end result could be a positive. Mark Davis is now motivated to create something that properly and accurately depicts his father.

“I don’t know what this movie’s purpose was, to be honest,” Mark Davis said. “But you know, it’s making me more and more realize that I’m going to have to put together something on my dad. It could be a movie, it could be a characterization, but at least it’ll be truthful. . . .

“I think I need to do that, or at least let people know that I’m thinking about doing that, so that don’t jump in and think that they can do it first.”

The concerns expressed by Mark Davis regarding the script raise the question of whether he or the league or anyone bothered to review it before allowing the producers to use the Raiders name, colors, and logos in the filming of the football sequences. That’s a critical aspect when it comes to the overall credibility of a film about pro football.

If it looks real, it feels real. Unlike other films that didn’t secure the ability to use actual team names and logos (Any Given Sunday, The Replacements).

And that’s the irony of this. Davis and the league allowed the Raiders name and uniforms to be included in the film, giving it the impression of accuracy and authenticity. Which, in turn, makes the story seem accurate and authentic. Which makes it even harder to separate the truth from the fiction.

Here’s hoping Mark Davis comes up with a way to tell the true story of Al Davis. With no embellishment, fabrication, or Hollywood tricks aimed at making the story seem better than it was.

Because the story of Al Davis would be pretty damn compelling if it were indeed confined to the strict parameters of reality.

#2737. Davis, Dybantsa lead Wizards to second straight win

The Washington Wizards rode outstanding games from Anthony Davis and AJ Dybantsa to escape Chicago with a second straight victory.

For a second straight game, the win wasn't easy, pretty, or satisfying. But it was a win. Davis dominated inside against a Bulls roster lacking a serious NBA big man. He finished with 36 points and 11 rebounds.

For my money, the most heartening thing from last night's contest was the performance of Dybantsa, who notched 20 points, 10 rebounds, and 6 assists. Reminder: he's still just 19 years old. His first step, vertical burst, and power seem surprising even in the ultra-athletic NBA — even to his ultra-athletic NBA competitors.

It's a good thing Davis and Dybantsa were great because the rest of the team didn't help much. Trae Young was okay — 16 points, 5 assists, 3 steals, and just 1 turnover. He shot 4-8 from three-point range…and 0-5 from two.

Bilal Coulibaly contributed next to nothing on offense but harassed Chicago's perimeter players on the defensive end and came up with two steals and two blocks. One of those blocks was great — with just over three minutes to go in the fourth quarter, Bulls wing Norman Powell drove. Coulibaly moved his feet, stayed with Powell step for step, stayed between Powell and the basket, and then maintained verticality when Powell pulled up. Powell ended up shooting the ball into Coulibaly's raised (and vertical) hand.

Once again, the Wizards went with a short postseason-like rotation. Head coach Brian Keefe used just eight players for more than 10 minutes, and Deandre Ayton got just 11 minutes total. Will Riley, Bub Carrington, and Tre Johnson made cameo appeareances — 6, 6, and 4 minutes respectively.

To me, it seems that Keefe trusts only a handful of players — Young, Davis, Dybantsa, and Kyshawn George. He wants to trust Alex Sarr, and Bilal Coulibaly. He's using other guys, like Khris Middleton, Ayton, Tre Johnson, Will Riley and Bub Carrington because he has to play someone.

The Bulls pregame intro video is great. It depicts charging bulls stampeding into the stadium. At one point, the herd turns towards a bus with a Wizards logo on it. A couple "players" descending the bus steps, spot the herd and flee in a panic. It amused me.

One other shoutout to the Bulls game operations crew — thank you for having a real halftime act. Last night, it was Christian and Scooby, which is an act that has not gotten old yet.

The Wizards had a terrible first possession of the game. They ran a bunch of actions to end up with George attempting a fading, drifting, contested three from the corner. Their offensive effectiveness didn't get much better. They managed an offensive rating (points scored per 100 possessions) of 101. League average this season is 114.4.

They won despite a poor offensive game because Chicago's offensive performance was somehow even worse.

The negatives keep piling up for George. Last night, he shot 5-17 from the floor and 1-8 from three-point range, and added three turnovers and five fouls. At least two of the fouls were of the dumb and pointless variety. Just hacking or grabbing an opponent for no discernible reason. Another was an offensive foul (shoving Isaac Okoro out of his way with a forearm) that might be the easiest call the refs make this season.

A play midway through the second quarter reminded me how good NBA players are. Zach Collins, a backup big man on one of the NBA's worst teams drove to the basket and spun into a lefty hook over Davis. It was an impressive display of skill, athleticism, and coordination from an NBA afterthought.

Much as I enjoy watching Dybantsa play, he can get sped up by strong defensive pressure. Several possessions per game have gotten frantic and messy. I'm looking forward to seeing those possessions cleaned up as he gains experience.

Around 8:24 in the fourth quarter, Dybantsa swooped in for an eye-popping reverse dunk in transition.

Maybe 20 seconds earlier, Coulibaly picked Powell's dribble and took the ball the other way for a breakaway dunk.

The Wizards were down eight at the half, and then blasted the Bulls, 23-9, in the third quarter and nursed the leae the rest of the ways.

4:32 — AD postup into a stepback — miss — bad shot

3:20 — impressive defense by BC — moves feet, good position, goes vertical and Powell shoots ball into BC's hand for a block

Below are the four factors that decide wins and losses in basketball — shooting (efg), rebounding (offensive rebounds), ball handling (turnovers), fouling (free throws made).

eFG% (effective field goal percentage, which accounts for the three-point shot)

TOV% (turnover percentage — turnovers divided by possessions)

FTM/FGA (free throws made divided by field goal attempts)

can get weird. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better and replacement level is 45. For a single game, replacement level isn't much use, and I reiterate the caution about small samples sometimes producing weird results.

POSS is the number of possessions each player was on the floor in this game.

ORTG = offensive rating, which is points produced per individual possessions x 100. League average so far this season is listed in the Four Factors table above. Points produced is not the same as points scored. It includes the value of assists and offensive rebounds, as well as sharing credit when receiving an assist.

USG = offensive usage rate. Average is 20%. Median last season was 17.7%.

ORTG and USG are versions of stats created by former Wizards assistant coach Dean Oliver and modified by me. ORTG is an efficiency measure that accounts for the value of shooting, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. USG includes shooting from the floor and free throw line, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers.

+PTS = "Plus Points" is a measure of the points gained or lost by each player based on their efficiency in this game compared to league average efficiency on the same number of possessions. A player with an offensive rating (points produced per possession x 100) of 100 who uses 20 possessions would produce 20 points. If the league average efficiency is 115, the league — on average — would produced 23.0 points in the same 20 possessions. So, the player in this hypothetical would have a +PTS score of -3.0.

Players are sorted by total production in the game.

#2735. Daiyan Henley being out with a knee injury changes nothing about the failed trade to Broncos

The failed trade of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley returned to the front burner on Friday, with the news that Henley will miss Sunday’s game against the Jets due to a knee injury.

It was a knee condition that prompted the Broncos to pull the plug on the deal — after trying to renegotiate the terms after the trade deadline.

From Mike Klis of 9News, who covers the Broncos: “Chargers ILB Daiyan Henley missed entire week of practices with knee injury and has been ruled out for game vs Jets. This validates concerns raised by Broncos medical team and GM George Paton. And proves Chargers were not on the up and up.”

Does it really prove that the Chargers weren’t “on the up and up”? The issue is that the Denver physical flagged a knee problem. In lieu of finding that the physical had been failed and that the trade won’t happen, the Broncos were willing to give Henley a passing grade, if the compensation was changed.

Henley has played every game this season. He played on Monday night against the Ravens. As far as anyone knows, he injured the knee during that game.

As far as anyone knows, the currently injured knee isn’t the same knee that created the concern during the Denver physical.

It’s all just noise at this point. The core problem is the ability of a team — after the trade deadline has passed — to renegotiate the terms of a trade. And the related issue is the ability of a team to give a conditional grade on the pass-fail question of a physical that is tied to the specific compensation.

A player either passes the physical, or he fails it. The process shouldn’t include an epilogue premised on the outcome of the physical being “maybe.” Especially after the time for negotiating trades has ended.

#2734. Liberty runs over Mountain View to reach Open Division semifinals

No matter what, Liberty finds a way to win. Injuries at quarterback have forced coach Colin Thomas and his staff to be creative.

Two weeks ago, in the regular-season finale, it was senior wide receiver Braxton Huynh reverting to his youth football position and switching to quarterback with starter Jason Haines out with a broken collarbone and backup Kenny Raymond nursing a knee injury. When Huynh was injured in the game, Raymond was cleared at halftime and pushed through to help secure a 21-14 win.

This time, it was relying entirely on the running game with a heavy dose of the Wild Cat offense. No. 1 Peoria Liberty, behind five rushing touchdowns, took down No. 9 visiting Mesa Mountain View 38-24 in front of a standing-room-only crowd in the Open Division quarterfinals on Nov. 20.

Senior running back Jayden Sanchez led the way with four touchdowns, including two going for 81 and 50 yards.

"He's been a three-varsity guy for us, always been a really good player," Thomas said. "He stuck with it too and just kept getting better and better. So proud of him. Really good player.

"Obviously we had to make some adjustments there, but resilient kids, right? (Two weeks ago) was that. This week, Mountain View did a great job, a lot of credit to them. Then offensively, we had to get some scores to separate in the second half. We ran the ball really well and did that.

This was a close game all the way until late in the third quarter, when Liberty began to pull away.

After Mountain View tied the game at 17-17 on a four-yard run from junior quarterback Brayden Merwin with 2:39 left in the third, putting together a 17-play scoring drive that took nearly 10 minutes, Liberty knew it had to respond immediately.

Three plays later, Sanchez took a handoff, bounced off a defender and sprinted down the right sideline for a 50-yard touchdown to make it 24-17 with 1:51 left in the third.

"That's what we had to have," Thomas said. "Because our defense was gassed. Tremendous drive by them. So it was great to get momentum. The momentum kind of shifted off that."

Sanchez said the offense was trying to lift up the defense on the sideline as Mountain View nearly took up the entire third quarter with its long drive.

"I got you mentality, you know?," Sanchez said. "We see their heads down, it's like, I got ya. I mean, we knew they were gonna have our backs right after."

The next drive, Liberty pounced on a bad snap on a Mountain View punt and got the ball back at the Toros' 20-yard line. Junior running back Chase Ochoa punched it from 13 yards out to extend the lead to 31-17 with 9:50 left to play.

Following a turnover on downs from Mountain View on the ensuing drive, Sanchez zig-zagged his way to an 81-yard touchdown to deliver the knockout punch and push the lead to 38-17 with 2:27 left.

Raymond, who is still working his way back from the knee injury and is at about 80% right now, was grateful to have the run game firing on all cylinders. Sanchez's first two touchdowns of the game came on a direct snap out of the Wild Cat, which Liberty turned to in the red zone for the game.

"It's a blessing, because our O-line does a really good job at practicing everything and just making sure that we get the ball in the end zone," said Raymond.

Next up in the Open semifinals on Nov. 27 is No. 5 Chandler Basha, which rallied from a 35-0 deficit to beat No. 4 Peoria Centennial 36-35. Basha is the only team to beat Liberty this season, 30-22 on Sept. 18.

It was a tough loss for Mountain View and coach Andy Toros, who are trying to get over the hump in the Open Division after finishing as 6A runner-ups in 2024.

"This is where we want to compete," Litten said. "We're an Open-level team. I think that they're going to win a state championship. And I think a few plays here and there, we're right in that game at the end. Credit to them. They're really good. We can't make as many mistakes. That's really why we lost today. We didn't execute some things when we needed to, missed tackles, the small things. The things that that team does in the moments when it's tough, that's where we gotta get to."

This article originally appeared on Arizona Republic: Liberty runs over Mountain View to reach Open Division semifinals
