#2733. The Celtics, in all of their early-season glory, haven’t passed Brad Stevens’ test yet

We're about a fifth of the way through the 2026-27 Boston Celtics season.

So far, mostly so good. The Celtics are 11-4, which has them slotted second in the East behind the Philadelphia 76ers — whom they beat in comfortable fashion last week at Xfinity Mobile Arena, 123-101.

For you analytics heads out there, Boston ranks sixth in offensive rating, second in defensive rating, and second in net rating.

Paul George, whom the Cs bet on when they traded Jaylen Brown for him (and some nice picks) couldn't be playing much better. If you need any insight into how the PG-13 Experience has been, look no further than the fanbase collectively referring to him as "Paul God."

The other offseason addition hasn't panned out as well, but we won't jump on the pile here.

Through this first month, the only real nitpick about this team is the schedule that they've had. Multiple games against the putrid Milwaukee Bucks and Chicago Bulls, plus a handful against other struggling squads like the Charlotte Hornets, Dallas Mavericks, Toronto Raptors, and Brooklyn Nets make the 11-4 record feel a bit inflated.

Don't take my word for it; here's what Brad Stevens had to say about last season's 56-win team in his end-of-season press conference.

"We have to play well in the regular season to get to where we want to go," he told reporters back in May. "We don't want to undersell the regular season. That said, as I look at us honestly, I look at how we played against the best teams is relevant and should be taken into account as we look at our team moving forward."

Boston's record against the top three teams in each conference was 3-11. Of course, their first-round loss to the 76ers only amplified that issue. The Sixers weren't a "top team" but at full-strength (which they miraculously were in Games 4-7), they're not your typical Play-In team.

Anyway, there was a clear correlation in all the losses vs. that in the wins. Boston shot just 27.4% from three in the losses. In victories, that number jumped up to 41.7%.

This season, they haven't quite shown us that it'll be a different story just yet. The Cs have had five games against teams above .500 and have won just two. Their three losses came agains the Detroit Pistons, Houston Rockets, and Denver Nuggets.

The two wins have featured elite shooting performances from the perimeter. Boston sank 16-40 in their home opener against the New York Knicks, and then lit the Sixers up with a 22-49 performance in Philly.

Somehow, they lost the opener against Detroit despite a strong shooting day, but the other two losses have gone exactly how you'd guess.

I know how this all sounds, too. Like yeah, of course they're going to shoot better in wins than losses — you could probably pull up the splits for every team in the league and they'd look the same.

With the Celtics, though, it's #DifferentHere. A team that's relied so heavily on winning the mathematical margins over the past four seasons has seen shooting variance end three of them in disappointing fashion. The 2024 team was special, but also managed to win playoff games when they went cold — even they dropped a few headscratchers thanks to variance.

Does this all mean that this season's team sucks?

Probably not. But it's disappointing that they've come up short a few times in their limited amount of "prove it" games. Their lost to Houston did come on the second night of a back-to-back where Paul God was resting. So, there's some grace to be given there.

One optimistic takeaway so far has been the elite defense. Boston's 106.0 defensive rating has been built on sharp rotations, disruptive defensive playmaking, and a strong paint presence from Neemias Queta. All three of those things will remain under their control regardless of whether or not the shots are going in on a given night.

The Celtics have held opponents to under 110 points in 11 of their 15 games thus far. By doing so, they're at least giving themselves a chance to get across the finish line when the threes don't fall. We might be watching them develop their backup plan in real time.

It's going to be a while before another "test" game. Their NBA Cup group stage finale against the Atlanta Hawks will be a minor test before they head to San Antonio to take on the Spurs next Sunday. A win against Wemby and the reigning West champs would go along way in battling the "schedule merchants" narratives.

#2730. From 1-5 to above .500, the Suns are doing something right

The Phoenix Suns are a game above .500. When this team started the season 1-5, I wasn't entirely convinced I'd have the opportunity to type those words anytime soon. Yet here we are, thanks to some improved chemistry, particularly among the starting unit, and a favorable stretch of the schedule.

How much of this resurgence can be attributed to genuine improvement versus the quality of competition? Only time will tell. We spend so much time dissecting how games are won or lost that we occasionally lose sight of a rather important detail. A win is a win. And in the NBA, every single one of them matters.

Yes, the Suns defeated the Utah Jazz by 10 points on Friday night, despite allowing Utah to trim the deficit to four in the closing minutes. Naturally, some will point to that late surge as evidence that this wasn't a particularly impressive victory. The funny thing? Many of those same people will dismiss Wednesday's win over the Sacramento Kings because, well, that's what the Suns were supposed to do. Don't be that guy.

Phoenix put itself in a position to win on Friday night, although Utah certainly helped the cause by missing 13 free throws. The result? A third consecutive road victory and a team that suddenly finds itself on the right side of .500.

Winning in the NBA is hard. I don't care who you're playing, how many injuries the opposing team is dealing with, or how ugly the basketball might look at times. Every team in this league has talented players capable of making your life miserable on any given night. Funny how that works, too. When an undermanned opponent beats the Suns, we're quick to praise their resilience and talk about how there's still some fight in that dog. But when Phoenix beats an undermanned opponent, suddenly the victory comes with an asterisk in the court of public opinion.

The win over Utah wasn't necessarily pretty. Some stretches made you uncomfortable, moments that invited frustration, and a fourth quarter that probably didn't need to be as interesting as it became. But it was effective. It added another victory to the win column, extended the momentum of a successful road trip, and gave the Suns something positive to carry into Monday's matchup against the New Orleans Pelicans.

It certainly beats the alternative. Never forget that alternative, either. Because if the Suns had blown that lead and lost to Utah, we'd be spending the next 48 hours dissecting every possession, questioning every rotation decision, and wondering whether this team had learned a damn thing from its early struggles.

Instead? Good win. Hop on the plane. On to the next city.

#2729. What happened to quarterback Julian Sayin? Will he return to Ohio State football?

Ohio State continues its season without starting quarterback Julian Sayin, who has an undisclosed injury to his throwing arm and will miss the Nov. 21 game at Nebraska.

In the fourth quarter of a a 19-15 win at Indiana on Oct. 17, Sayin was hurt when he was sacked early in the fourth quarter. Defensive lineman Mario Landino collided with Sayin as he began to attempt a pass, causing his arm to bend awkwardly.

Sayin had to exit the game early. After leaving for the locker room, he returned with his right throwing arm in a sling. Quarterback Luke Fahey finished the fourth quarter for OSU and started in losses to USC and Oregon and last week's win over Northwestern.

Sayin has been behind center for the Buckeyes for more than a year, having made 21 consecutive starts since he beat out Lincoln Kienholz in a preseason competition in 2025.

More: How Ohio State football QB Luke Fahey got the chance to fulfill a childhood dream

Sayin finished fourth in the voting for the Heisman Trophy last year with one of the most accurate single seasons for a passer in the Football Bowl Subdivision. Over his two seasons as the starter, he has thrown for 5,617 yards with 51 touchdowns and 12 interceptions.

Ohio State football's future at quarterback has been murky since Sayin got hurt. Will his injury make him more likely to stay in college rather than leave early for the NFL?

Sayin, 21, has two more years of college eligibility after this season. He was originally recruited by Alabama, but when program legend Nick Saban retired from coaching after the 2023-24 season, Sayin entered the transfer portal. Sayin appeared in four games as a backup to Will Howard during Ohio State's national championship season, and so he was able to redshirt that year under the rules applicable at the time.

Sayin has the option to forgo his eligibility and declare for the 2027 NFL Draft, but whether he will do so is far harder to predict now than it was a few weeks ago.

Before the injury, The Athletic's draft analysts had a hard time projecting where Sayin would end up.

"Scouting Sayin independently from Smith, the No. 1 player in the 2027 NFL Draft class, is not easy. You don't penalize the quarterback because of the talent at receiver, but [Jeremiah] Smith is the biggest cheat code in the sport," wrote Dane Brugler on Oct. 4.

Brugler praised Sayin's accuracy and highlighted his strong sense of rhythm, as well as his ability to exploit vulnerable areas on pre-snap reads. On the other hand, he noted Sayin could be inconsistent when under pressure in the pocket.

"Sayin has an NFL future, no doubt about it. But convincing NFL teams he is a first-rounder and a starter will take more work," Brugler wrote.

The Athletic draft analyst Nick Baumgardner agreed that Sayin's draft profile is difficult to quantify.

"When you stack him against the other top draft-eligible arms, he lands toward the back of the pack," Baumgardner wrote on Oct. 4. "He's not real big, and his arm strength is pretty limited. He's very smart, though. He knows where to go with the ball, doesn't get stuck too much and can be really accurate."

Even before Sayin's injury, one draft profile from CBS Sports speculated that Sayin might want to consider one more year with the Buckeyes.

"There's actually a reasonable case that Sayin could improve his stock by proving that he's not only a Jeremiah [Smith] merchant and can go through reads and quarterback at a high level," wrote Shehan Jeyarajah on Sept. 28. "Of course … there's always the possibility that he is a Jeremiah merchant, and his production (and draft stock) falls off a cliff when he's gone.

Since Sayin's injury, however, not many analysts have considered Sayin as part of next year's draft class.

Given all the uncertainty, it would be unsurprising to see Sayin come back for another year of college football.

If Sayin does return to Ohio State, it also seems likely that he would regain his starting role. His backup, Fahey, has struggled to throw passes downfield in his first two starts.

Ohio State could always test the waters of the transfer portal for a quarterback, but the position is expensive. Howard, the Buckeyes' national championship-winning quarterback, told The Athletic that the NIL deal he received after he transferred from Kansas State was worth seven figures.

On top of that, Sayin has started 21 games for the Buckeyes and was a Heisman Trophy finalist season his first full year. It would be a shock if Ohio State willingly moved on from the signal caller rather than accepting him back with open arms.

Fahey was a three-star recruit and the No. 35 quarterback in the 2026 class, according to 247Sports' composite rankings. He quickly stepped up as a freshman and lost his black stripe following the Buckeyes' first preseason intrasquad scrimmage on Aug. 15.

At the beginning of preseason training camp, Day praised Fahey's development.

"He's really been doing a great job," Day said in August. "He's putting a lot of pressure on Tavien. He really is. He's been competing. He's been making plays."

Before camp, it was presumed that quarterback Tavien St. Clair would move up after spending last year as the third-stringer. St. Clair stood out during the spring game in April. The native of Bellefontaine, who was the first Ohio high school quarterback since Joe Burrow to sign a scholarship agreement with Ohio State, was a highly touted five-star prospect.

In the week leading up to Ohio State's season opener, Day said that St. Clair and Fahey would continue to split reps with the second-team offense in practices leading up to the game. By the time the Ball State game came around on Sept. 5, it was Fahey, not St. Clair, who entered the contest when Sayin's day was done.

In seven games, Fahey has completed 87 of 133 passes (65.4%) for 1,024 yards, eight touchdowns and four interceptions. He has 19 carries for 15 yards.

When St. Clair signed his scholarship agreement in 2024, he became the first Ohio-based quarterback to do so since Joe Burrow in 2015.

A five-star recruit out of Bellefontaine High School, St. Clair was the second-ranked quarterback from the Class of 2024, according to 247Sports, slotting behind Michigan's Bryce Underwood.

touchdowns and four interceptions that season, marking the second-consecutive year he hit the 2,000-yard mark.

St. Clair ended as the runner-up for the Mr. Football title, as junior quarterback Matt Ponatoski out of Cincinnati Moeller beat him out by 10 points (70-60).

St. Clair spent his freshman season behind Sayin and Lincoln Kienholz, who transferred to Louisville during the offseason, in the quarterback rotation, but made an appearance in the Buckeyes' 70-0 win over Grambling State. St. Clair logged 13 snaps against the Tigers, going 0 for 2.

St. Clair holds a significant size advantage over Fahey, standing at 6 feet 4, 195 pounds. Fahey is 5-11, 206..

#2728. One ‘insane’ five-minute stretch shows just how lost Mitchell Robinson is with Celtics

Mitchell Robinson looks like his heart is still in New York.

The Celtics' free-agent acquisition has looked lost in Boston this season, struggling on both ends of the floor and turning the ball over at a career-high rate.

Robinson's troubles reached a new level during a bizarre stretch Wednesday in the third quarter of an eventual 105-101 Nuggets victory.

"Robinson wasn't ready for it on the short roll," play-by-play man Mike Monaco said on the broadcast.

Boston Celtics center Mitchell Robinson, front, goes to the basket as Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic chases him on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, in Denver. AP Photo/David Zalubowski

"And I don't know if that was a great pass to Mitchell Robinson on the roll," Richard Jefferson said on the call. "I don't think that's the best place to utilize him."

The Celtics had nine turnovers in the third quarter, and while only one was credited to Robinson officially, he was involved in at least three of them.

One was an offensive foul due to a moving screen (officially given to Payton Pritchard) and two of the others were due to poor communication between him and the ball handlers.

On one sequence with six minutes remaining in the third quarter, Robinson mishandled a pick-and-roll pass, leading to a dunk at the other end for Denver.

Paul George later attempted a pass to him wide open under the basket but Robinson stopped his movement early, and the ball sailed into the stands, drawing a few comments and confused looks from George.

Then with roughly 2:40 remaining in the quarter, Robinson was switching off a cutting Christian Braun for an easy basket.

Robinson was immediately given the hook after that play, after playing roughly five minutes in a disaster quarter, with Robinson's picks heavily involved in plays that ended in turnovers.

Perhaps coach Joe Mazzulla is having a tough time figuring out how to use Robinson, as he may not be the best fit as a rim runner and pick-and-roll specialist for dunks and passes to slashers.

Boston Celtics center Mitchell Robinson has been a turnover machine this season posting career-worst numbers. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

"I think he's playing a role that we need him to play. It's bigs by committee," Mazzulla said after Monday's 115-105 loss to the Magic.

After a poor outing Monday, Robinson admitted that "I could've done better tonight."

Those watching — including Sam Vecenie, host of the basketball podcast "Game Theory" — felt a little more strongly.

"I am truly blown away by the five minutes that Mitchell Robinson played in the 3rd quarter for Boston against Denver last night," Vecenie said of Robinson. "That was insane."

Payton Pritchard and head coach Joe Mazzulla of the Boston Celtics look on during a game against the Denver Nuggets on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, in Denver. NBAE via Getty Images

Robinson's struggles go well beyond that, though. He has posted a terrible -30 plus-minus during his 246 minutes on the floor for the Celtics this year.

With him off the floor, the Celtics are +191, a massive 221-point swing.

Robinson has career-lows in rebounds per game (5.4) and an alarming 2.4 offensive rebounds per game, compared to 4.2 last year in just two fewer minutes per game for the Knicks' title team.

He's also posted a career-high 0.9 turnovers per game, and he has by far his lowest block and steal rates.

It will be interesting to see how Mazzulla gets Robinson acclimated, as he signed a three-year, $47.38 million contract this offseason. He was the one significant piece to leave the Knicks' title team as they were hellbent on not flirting with the second apron.

Celtics super fan Bill Simmons posted his concerns on X on Friday.

"'Mitchell Robinson will be fine, settle down, he just needs to play himself into shape' — a text I've sent 52 times this season already," Simmons said in a social media post.

The Celtics have been better without Mitchell Robinson on the floor. AP Photo/David Zalubowski

The Knicks have, in turn, replaced him with Andre Drummond, who is mostly there for rebounding, while former Warriors draft bust James Wiseman has also been getting some minutes at center.

The Celtics are 11-4, while the Knicks are 9-6.

#2722. Cy Young winners Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler just put up a 2026 tandem not seen since 1905

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

To no one's real surprise, Jacob Misiorowski of the Milwaukee Brewers and Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees have been named the 2026 Cy Young Award winners for, respectively, the National League and American League. Each was announced as the winner of Major League Baseball's topmost honor for pitchers, and each won the balloting in unanimous fashion. They are the first duo to win unanimously in the same year in their respective leagues since Justin Verlander and Sandy Alcantara in 2022 and just the third in MLB history.

Obviously, Cy Young winners have necessarily authored excellent seasons, but in the case of this year's winners, the descriptor "excellent" doesn't quite rise to meet the work of Misiorowski and Schlittler:

We could get into stuff, yes, as each has a blazing fastball that overwhelms hitters at the front end of a deep repertoire. This exercise, though, is more about how Misiorowski and Schlittler have overwhelmed the opposition when it comes to keeping runs off the board. You'll note all the strikeouts above, of course, but what may catch the eye is that each boasts a sub-2.00 ERA. That's a time-honored signifier of pitcher impeccability, even if ERA has its flaws.

To upgrade this familiar stat just a bit – and to put the two 2026 Cy Young winners' accomplishments into fitting context – we'll turn to ERA+. ERA+ is ERA adjusted to reflect league and home ballpark tendencies. An ERA+ of 100 represents the league average, and each point above or below that mark reflects a one-point change. For example, a pitcher with an ERA+ of 120 had a park- and league-adjusted ERA that was 20% better than the league average, while a pitcher with an ERA+ of 95 was 5% worse than the league average. So from the hurlers' standpoint, the higher the ERA+, the better.

This is all a necessary step when comparing pitchers across eras, because run–scoring environments have changed so drastically over the history of the sport. For example, Pedro Martinez's ERA of 1.74 in 2000, when teams were averaging more than five runs per game, means a lot more than, say, Charlie Chech's 1.74 ERA in 1908, when teams averaged 3.38 runs per game. That's where ERA+ comes in. Martinez in 2000 had an ERA+ of 291, or a park-adjusted ERA that was 191% (!) better than the league average. Chech in 1908 had the same ERA as Martinez in 2000, but his ERA+ of 136 was drastically worse.

As for the two moundsmen of present interest, Misiorowski this past season had an ERA+ of 232, which led the majors. Schlittler had an ERA+ of 215, which led the American League. Yes, they had those sub-2.00 ERAs, but, really, topping a 200 ERA+ is a much more impressive achievement. Counting Misiorowski and Schlittler but throwing out the pitchers who achieved the mark in the 60-game 2020 season (you should always throw out 2020), just 43 pitchers in MLB since 1900 have managed a 200 ERA+ or better across a qualifying number of innings. Over that same span and with 2020 also omitted, 201 pitchers have achieved a sub-2.00 ERA in a qualifying number of innings.

As you can imagine, it's a rarity to have not one but two pitchers in the same season who have a 200 ERA+ or better, as was the case this past season with Misiorowski and Schlittler. How rare? No season has ever given us more than two such qualifiers. Here's the full list of those across all of modern MLB history (i.e., since 1900):

Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers (232); Cam Schlittler, Yankees (215)

Jacob deGrom, Mets (218); Blake Snell, Rays (217)

Jake Arrieta, Cubs (215), Zack Greinke, Dodgers (222)

Roger Clemens, Blue Jays (222); Pedro Martinez, Expos (219)

Carl Lundgren, Cubs (211); Jack Pfiester, Cubs (214)

Christy Mathewson, Giants (233); Ed Reulbach, Cubs (209)

Yes, just six seasons have given us more than one 200 ERA+ pitcher, and this year's Miz-Cam combo marks just the third time that we've had one from each league. Accordingly, this marks just the third time that each Cy Young winner has reached the 200 ERA+ benchmark in a given season.

There's another, even more exclusive group that puts the Miz-Cam tandem in the proper context and hints at a future that's as bright as their present and their recent past. In 2026, Schlittler was in his age-25 campaign, while Misiorowski was in his age-24 season. So they're young as frontline aces go, and while you never want to make assumptions about pitcher health and durability in the current era, this duo's elite performance at both top-line and underlying level raises the possibility that each will win another Cy or two (or three) in the years to come.

Turning back to the 200 ERA+ defining stat, such youth in tandem with such excellence is all but unprecedented. Of the seasons listed just above, just 1905 featured two pitchers who, like Miz and Cam this past season, were age 25 or younger at the time. Mathewson, the inner-circle all-time great, was 24 that season and Reulbach was a 22-year-old rookie. We haven't seen something like that in more than 120 years.

Let's also note that Misiorowski and Shlittler, who each struck out more than 30% of opposing batters this season, absolutely have the stuff and foundational, forward-looking results to continue lording over their guild. Until that comes to pass, though, let's appreciate ther historical rare success and their even more historically rare combination of success and youth.

#2721. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2716. Yaxel Lendeborg, Warriors get a taste of life without Stephen Curry: 'It felt helpless out there'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Warriors went into survival mode the minute it was announced that Stephen Curry would miss at least the next two weeks, and perhaps more, with an oblique tear. And in their first test, Curry's absence was felt in a major way as the Spurs put a 38-point beating on them on Friday night.

This was never going to end well. The Warriors would have been heavy underdogs in this game even had Curry played. But the Warriors were hoping to at least stay in the fight for a little while. Instead, they were the Michael Spinks to San Antonio's Mike Tyson as the Spurs scored the first 18 points of the game and never looked back.

There are a few core things that need to happen for the Warriors to stay competitive while Curry is out, and it starts with Yaxel Lendeborg assuming full-time alpha status and producing like an All-Star with the defense now primarily focused on him.

It's a lot to ask of a rookie, but he's set the bar so high to start his career that he's proven capable. He's putting up north of 20 points per game on super efficient shooting through his first 12 games.

Could he possibly do it again against the Spurs? The answer was an emphatic no. Lendeborg had three points on 1-of-13 shooting, and afterward he was beating himself up worse than the Spurs did.

"We just got the s--t beat out of us," Lendeborg said. "I was flustered the entire game. I couldn't make a damn layup. I don't even know, man. ... I'm not going to move past this. Everybody is saying throw it out the window. I can't throw a damn thing out the window. We just lost by like a hundred. I'm f--ked up mentally right now.

"It was an awful performance by me," Lendeborg continued. "I let everybody on this team down. I'm not gonna forget this ever. I don't remember the last time I got beat [like this] the whole entire game, with no hope at all. It felt helpless out there."

Helpless. It's a strong word, but appropriate on this night. Welcome to life without the greatest shooter and one of the greatest scorers to ever live commanding all the defensive attention and still putting up 30 a night.

Lendeborg's unfiltered commentary is refreshingly raw. He says exactly what is on his mind, and certainly you'd rather have a player be hard on himself after a performance like this than a guy who doesn't care. But it was, in the end, one game against probably the best team with the best player in the world.

Lendeborg will be fine. If you're thinking he got exposed in this game, save it. This dude is for real. He'll discard this and get right for New Orleans on Monday, because at 8-5 the Warriors are still in good shape. They can't let this spiral and suddenly the next few weeks are undoing all the good work they did to start the season.

Steve Kerr started small against Victor Wembanyama, inserting De'Anthony Melton and Will Richard into the first five with Draymond Green at center. Bold move. The only way that can work is to run and gun, and Brandin Podziemski needed to be at the forefront of that attack. He wasn't.

Podziemski, who has been terrific to start the season, averaging nearly 17 points per game and hitting 2.8 3-pointers a night at a 40% clip, finished with eight points on 2-of-10 shooting in San Antonio. Do the math, and Podziemski and Lendeborg, the Warriors' top two offensive options in Curry's absence, combined to miss 20 of 23 shots.

There's some reason for hope with this duo as this Curry-less stretch continues. This season, they have led the Warriors to a +2.6 net rating in their minutes without Curry, via Databallr. It's a very different story doing it without Curry for a few minutes while he rests on the bench, versus doing it for full games. But there's no time for learning curves here. This duo probably needs to score 40 points and create closer to 60 without Curry.

The Warriors need to win in New Orleans on Monday. The Pelicans are kind of a mess right now, and Golden State getting to 9-5 would go a long way toward at least allowing Curry to return to a .500 team. After facing the Pelicans, the Warriors play the Mavericks and Grizzlies on a back-to-back, and then the Celtics in their first game back home. It's a hard stretch.

After that, it's the Kings on Nov. 25, which will be the two-week mark of Curry's timeline. The Warriors will cross their fingers that he can come back after that game, and in that case, even if they only beat the Pelicans and Kings over this stretch, they would still be 10-8 upon Curry's return.

Even if Curry ends up missing an extra week or so, two of the Warriors' three games following the Kings matchup come against the 3-8 Clippers (who they have already beaten without Curry) and the 1-12 Jazz. They can still come out of this OK.

#2715. 2. Bundesliga: Hannover leave it late to snatch dramatic victory over Fürth

Sandro Wagner's side looked set for another frustrating afternoon after struggling to break down a well-organised Fürth defence, but goals from Stefan Thordarson and Taibi ultimately secured all three points for the hosts.

Hannover made a positive start and thought they had a case for an early penalty when Benjamin Källman went down inside the penalty area after just four minutes. However, referee Marc Eckermann waved away the appeals, with the incident proving particularly costly for the hosts as Källman was unable to continue following the challenge.

Thordarson subsequently came on earlier than expected, but Hannover struggled to maintain their early momentum against a Fürth side that defended deep and looked to frustrate their opponents.

Despite offering little going forward during the opening stages, the visitors took the lead in the 34th minute. A short corner routine involving Luca Itter and Aaron Keller eventually saw Krisztian Keresztes deliver into the penalty area, where Ole Pohlmann was left unmarked to head home from close range.

Hannover struggled to find a response before the interval, with Wagner introducing Lars Gindorf at half-time in an attempt to inject some much-needed attacking impetus.

The hosts continued to look short of ideas after the restart, and the frustration around the stadium became increasingly apparent as Fürth comfortably dealt with their attacking attempts.

However, Hannover finally found a breakthrough in the 57th minute. Marcel Hartel combined with Gindorf before reaching the byline and pulling the ball back into the penalty area, where Thordarson was on hand to turn home the equaliser.

The goal provided Hannover with renewed hope, although their performance remained inconsistent as Fürth continued to threaten their chances of securing a comeback.

Gindorf was particularly influential after his introduction, offering a greater attacking threat than his teammates, but the hosts appeared destined to settle for a point as the match entered its closing stages.

That was until Taibi produced a moment of individual brilliance in the 92nd minute. Picking up the ball approximately 20 metres from goal, the midfielder unleashed a superb strike that flew into the net, leaving the Fürth goalkeeper with little chance and sending the home supporters into celebration.

The late winner secured a valuable three points for Hannover, who move up to 15 points, while Fürth remain on 12 after suffering another disappointing result on the road.

Hannover will look to carry their momentum into next weekend's trip to VfL Osnabrück, while Fürth return home to face Arminia Bielefeld.

#2714. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The big prize of this free agent class is ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. We've seen and will continue to see predictions that he's going to land a deal of around 8-10 years and topping $400 million. The knee-jerk reaction to such prognostications in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the signing team is getting a surefire ace for several years.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here says this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

Also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a new procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. If he signs an eight-year deal, it'll run through his age-37 season.

For those so worried about the long-term finances of the team owner who ends up signing Skubal, are you sure you're really worried that he won't be productive through five, six, seven or even all eight years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

Justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

David Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

By this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:

Are you sure a 10-year, $400 million deal for this guy would be a "risk?"

I think we could argue that it would be a bargain.

#2712. Championship hangover? Josh Hart 'not in a good headspace' as he, other Knicks struggle amid uneven start

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Knicks slipped to 6-6 on Friday with a 106-104 loss to the Indiana Pacers, dropping into a tie for fifth in the Eastern Conference alongside the Miami Heat.

While it hasn't been an outright disaster of a start, it has been an uneven performance by the defending champions that has left them frustrated and searching for answers. The championship hangover in New York seems to be real, and the once immaculate vibes at Madison Square Garden have been replaced by frustration as they try to get on track.

After a scoreless performance against the Pacers, Josh Hart was brutally honest about not knowing what's wrong and how he's been struggling mentally to start this season.

"Wish I could tell you," Hart said. "Don't know. Right now I'm not in a good headspace, and I got to figure out how to improve that and improve my play."

One of the strengths of the Knicks during their title run last year was their rotation of two-way wings between Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns, but so far this season their three best wings -- OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Hart -- have been stuck in the mud offensively.

Those three are all shooting below 40% from the field and below 33% from 3-point range this season, a massive departure from last season when they were all above 48% from the field and 37% from distance. The result of New York's wings struggling on offense -- aside from Landry Shamet, who has been a needed bright spot -- has been an even greater burden on Brunson and Towns.

Towns has been sensational, averaging 21.1 points and 13.7 rebounds per game on 54.2/40.0/77.0 shooting splits as he's moved back to a full-time role at center after the departure of Mitchell Robinson. Brunson has been his typically excellent self, averaging 26.6 points and 5.7 assists per game -- a slim uptick in points and a small decrease in assists from last year -- but his efficiency has dipped, shooting 43.6% from the field.

While his 3-point percentage has held firm at 37.5%, he's shooting just 55.8% from inside three feet. That would be the worst finishing rate of his career at the rim and seems to be a byproduct of teams collapsing in without the threat of spacing from the wings around Brunson.

A less effective Brunson at the rim, the struggles of their wings and Towns playing more at the five have resulted in a Knicks offense that is 29th in the NBA in paint points at 35.5%. Mike Brown's offense is predicated on launching threes, but a year ago the Knicks got 41.4% of their points in the paint. A 6% drop-off there is a significant reduction, especially considering how poorly they're shooting from three as a team.

The big question raised by Hart's comments after Indiana's game is: how did the Knicks get here after winning the title?

It's one thing to have a championship hangover, but it's another to have the vibes of a team sour so quickly, considering their success was built in no small part on being a tight-knit group. It's hard not to point to the top of the organization and the way James Dolan seemed adamant about raining on the Knicks' championship celebration almost as soon as it began.

Dolan didn't even let the champagne-soaked locker room dry out before he proclaimed his refusal to go into the second apron to keep the team together. He stayed true to his word, letting Robinson walk to the rival Boston Celtics. However, what was perhaps more impactful on this year's poor start is the way the Knicks handled extension talks with much of their roster.

Towns made clear his desire to work out a deal to stay in New York and cut the Knicks a hometown discount, but New York was asking him to take an even bigger pay cut than he was willing. Ultimately, talks fell apart and the Knicks made the curious decision to publicly announce they were no longer going to discuss extensions with anyone on the roster a week before the season began.

Hart is among the extension-eligible players, but unlike Towns, who can decline a player option and hit free agency, his option for next year is a $22.3 million team option. If the Knicks wanted, they could simply pick up Hart's option and extend discussions on a new deal into next summer. One can't help but wonder whether the uncertainty about the future is part of whatis affecting Hart and putting him in a bad headspace.

Some players thrive under the pressure of a contract year, while others just feel the anxiety of not having a stable future. Hart, whose impact often goes beyond the box score, might feel that more than others.

The Knicks had two paths they could've taken this summer after winning their first title in over 50 years. One was to do everything possible to lock up the core group as quickly as possible and try to keep the good vibes rolling. The other was to play hardball and use the championship as an opportunity to squeeze players for a discount.

Knicks fans weren't surprised to see Dolan choose option two, and now they have to wonder if that's at the root of an uneven start to their title defense.

Thursday marks the final day of the General Manager meetings in Las Vegas. Though we haven't seen any major moves this offseason, we have seen an uptick in rumors in the past few days and that isn't a coincidence. Put a bunch of reporters and front-office execs in the same area for three or four days and chatter picks up, even if there isn't a ton of actual substance behind it.

Rumors are always fun, so let's round up the latest right here in addition to any news.

We have one of our first major-league deals of the offseason as the Braves have signed reliever Evan Phillips to a three-year, $35 million deal. Phillips ranked No. 34 on our top 50 free agent list.

Phillips, a 32-year-old right-hander, has been a setup man or closer for the Dodgers for the last several seasons. In returning from surgery last season, he appeared in 31 games, pitching to a 3.46 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 33 strikeouts in 26 innings. The majority of his closing experience came in 2023 when he had 24 saves in 27 chances.

The Braves' closer last season was Raisel Iglesias, but he's a free agent. Holdover Robert Suarez could take over those duties while Phillips, lefty Dylan Lee and youngster Didier Fuentes are also in the late-inning mix.

The Blue Jays went from one of the best offensive teams in 2025 to one of the worst in 2026. They'd love a big bounceback from Vladimir Guerrero Jr., among other positive movements, but they also look for outside help. Might that help come in the form of free agent infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr.?

The Jays have met with representatives for Chisholm, reports Sportsnet.

Chisholm, 28, hit .231/.312/.399 last season, but had a huge 2025 and any signing team would be hoping for the 2025 version of Chisholm.

The Jays do have a capable incumbent second baseman in Ernie Clement, but either Clement or Chisholm can be used in the outfield and the Blue Jays certainly need outfield upgrades.

The Phillies have been telling opposing teams that they are not "locked into anything" regarding their current outfield situation, according to The Athletic, so much so that All-Star outfielder Brandon Marsh is available in a trade.

As things stand, with Bryce Harper moving back to first base, the Phillies would have Bryan De La Cruz in right, Justin Crawford in center and Marsh in left, but that all seems pretty fluid as they look to upgrade the ballclub and keep that window of contention open.

Marsh, 28, had a stellar start last season, leading to his first-ever All-Star Game. Through July 1, he hit .319/.352/.530. The rest of the way, however, he slashed .177/.241/.241, dragging him down overall to a 90 OPS+ and 0.4 WAR on the season.

The Mariners have shown interest in free agent left fielder Ian Happ, per MLB Network.

Happ, 32, has spent his entire 10-year MLB career with the Cubs, who drafted him in the first round all the way back in 2015. He was pretty consistent from 2022-25, averaging 3.9 WAR with a .251/.347/.433 (118 OPS+) line and winning four Gold Gloves. Last season, though, he dipped to .218/.326/.412 (103 OPS+) with 2.7 WAR. He still topped 20 home runs for the fifth time in the last six years.

The Mariners have a vacancy in left field with Randy Arozarena having hit free agency and a need to upgrade their offense.

Yesterday's big news was the Yankees' interest in free agent first/third baseman Alec Bohm and The Athletic reports that we can now add the Mets to the list of suitors.

Bohm hit .249/.315/.383 (87 OPS+) with 15 home runs, 88 RBI and -0.2 WAR last season. It might be surprising to see him garnering such interest on the open market, but there isn't much right-handed power out there and Bohm finished last season strong (.318/.402/.453 in his last 42 games). The Mets, meanwhile, are desperate for help at the cold corner after last year's disastrous Jorge Polanco experiment. Jared Young did provide a glimmer of hope at first base before suffering a concussion in September while colliding with a teammate on a play.

Free agent starting pitcher Dustin May has a decent market right now, according to MLB Network, with at least the Cubs, White Sox, Padres and Astros having shown interest in the right-hander.

May, 29, made 31 starts between the Cardinals and Brewers last season, going 7-9 with a 4.70 ERA in 145 ⅔ innings. He showed flashes of brilliance with the Cardinals and had a stretch from April 10 to June 15 during which he posted a 2.54 ERA in 12 starts, but in the end there was plenty of inconsistency and even bad, forcing him into a bullpen role in the playoffs for the champion Brewers.

Free agent catcher Ryan Jeffers has been extended the qualifying offer from the Twins, meaning he has to decide by net Tuesday whether to accept the one-year, $23.15 million contract or hit free agency. There's nothing that says a team can't re-sign a player after he declines their qualifying offer, of course, and it sounds like that path is possible in this case.

Jeffers will decline the QO and the Twins are interested in reaching a multi-year deal to bring him back, reports the Minnesota Star-Tribune. Jeffers hit .256/.353/.461 with 14 home runs for Minnesota in 2026, a standout line for a catcher, though he missed several months with a broken hamate. The Twins do have several catchers in their farm system, including Vahn Lackey, the No. 3 pick in last year's draft, and Eduardo Tait, who headlined the trade return for Jhoan Duran.

Much has been said and will continue to be said about the 2027 free agent class and how it looks relatively weak, especially on the position-player side, where the best players are the likes of Jazz Chisholm Jr., Seiya Suzuki, and the aforementioned Arozarena and Jeffers.

As we know, the Rays love to find avenues where they can exploit market inefficiencies. Their latest move might be to hit the trade market with center fielder Jonny DeLuca in anticipation of moving Victor Mesa Jr. to center, according to The Athletic.

DeLuca, 28, got more playing time than ever before in 2026, appearing in 112 games and getting 370 plate appearances. He hit .266/.300/.429 (101 OPS+) with 11 homers, 50 RBI, 17 steals and 1.7 WAR.

Fresh off a playoff berth despite the lowest payroll in all of baseball at a paltry $75ish million, the Guardians are planning to increase payroll. Or so they say.

"We'll go up," club president Chris Antonetti told The Athletic. "We have to."

The Guardians hosted six playoff games and made some money there, not to mention that they have a bunch of players hitting arbitration and surely they want to spend more to remain competitive. There's an added wrinkle here, too, which would be that the ownership side is really pushing hard for a salary cap when the upcoming CBA expires in a few weeks. With a cap comes a floor and we've seen MLB float proposals with salary floors in the $180 million range, or well more than double what the Guardians had last season.

So, yeah, I'd say the Guardians "have to" increase payroll, one way or another.

#2710. Sandpapergate fallout: Usman Khawaja, David Warner pulled from commentary duties amid fresh storm

The fallout from Australia's explosive Sandpapergate controversy has taken another turn, with broadcaster Fox Cricket taking former openers Usman Khawaja and David Warner off its commentary roster as fresh revelations about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continue to rock Australian cricket.Fox Sports managing director Steve Crawley confirmed that both commentators would be rested from broadcasts over the next few weeks, acknowledging that the continuing controversy had made it increasingly difficult for them to concentrate on their broadcasting responsibilities. No return date has been announced."In light of recent events, both Usman and Davey will be rested from our broadcasts over the next few weeks,'' Crawley told CODE Sports."While we always support all members of our commentary team and welcome a diversity of views, which is a feature of our summer of cricket, we also understand the pressure they are under to respond to every new comment," he added."We think it is increasingly difficult to focus on the game while the situation continues to unfold and think it is unfair on both commentators to put them in that position," he said."Our focus remains on providing our viewers with the best broadcast of Australia's summer of cricket. We will continue to monitor the situation," he concluded.

The controversy has resurfaced following revelations in Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr, and subsequent comments from Cameron Bancroft suggesting that knowledge of the ball-tampering plan extended beyond the three players who were initially sanctioned.Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball during the Cape Town Test against South Africa in March 2018. The scandal resulted in suspensions for then captain Steve Smith, vice-captain Warner and Bancroft, triggering one of the biggest crises in Australian cricket.In his autobiography, Khawaja questioned the extent of knowledge within the Australian dressing room about the plan. Bancroft subsequently added fuel to the controversy through a column in The West Australian, alleging that the wider squad was aware of what was happening and that discussions about generating reverse swing had involved members of the bowling group, including Pat Cummins.Bancroft described Cummins' recent press conference as the 'final straw' that prompted him to break his silence.

Cummins strongly rejected the allegations when questioned about them in Sydney, describing the suggestion that the entire team knew about the plan as "complete and utter nonsense".The renewed controversy has put Australia's Test captain under scrutiny, with questions emerging over his position amid the fresh claims. Cricket Australia, however, has backed Cummins to continue as skipper, issuing a statement of support.Australia face England in the first of five T20 Internationals at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on Saturday, before opening their home Test summer against New Zealand at Perth Stadium on December 9.

#2708. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Celtics win Jaylen Brown trade (for now), Trae Young looks done

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Every now and then, the NBA gives us a week that is essentially built around a single game. A total of 51 games were played in the last week, but come on, the one you remember was Jaylen Brown's long-awaited reunion with Jayson Tatum. The Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers squared off in a battle of the Eastern Conference's two top seeds on Tuesday, and even if the game fell short of our basketball expectations, it provided more than enough beef to sate us. Brown snubbed Tatum before the game. Paul George gave a fan the middle finger. Appropriate animosity has returned to this eternal rivalry.

So... how did we handle that from a winners and losers perspective? Well, Boston is an obvious winner, but Brown escaped loser status. It's winners and losers of the week. Philly won its two other games this week, and Brown led all scorers in Sunday's win with 31 points. He certainly lost on Tuesday. He may yet wind up losing the trade. But we're not docking him a whole week for a single poor performance. So if Brown escaped the loser's section, who made it? And who joins Boston in the winner's circle? Let's look back at the week that was.

Boston's big win over Philadelphia underlined something that's been evident all season: Paul George, at least thus far, has been better as a Celtic than Jaylen Brown has been as a 76er. There are obviously circumstantial reasons for that. George is at his best as a force-multiplier, and he's on a team on which he doesn't need to play an enormous role. Brown is at his best as a floor-raiser, but he's on a team full of floor-raisers. That doesn't mean Philadelphia regrets the trade -- it got them LeBron James! -- but it does suggest that, after months of criticism, the Celtics at least got what they were looking for out of the deal.

Everything the Celtics were good at a year ago, they're still good at. They were one of the NBA's best shooting teams last season, and George both makes more 3s than Brown and takes far more of them. They were great at protecting the basket last season and George's activity as a helper has been a net benefit to their rim-protection.

Yet George's presence has also been the catalyst for improvement in a few other key areas. Boston never generated turnovers defensively last season and they do this year, in part because George is averaging the sixth-most steals and third-most deflections in the NBA. They're getting to the line at a roughly league-average rate, in part because the ball doesn't stick to George as it so often did Brown. It's easier to get defenses in rotation with the ball moving and 3-pointers flying. Tatum has benefited enormously in this respect with a career-best 46% free-throw rate.

Again, the 76ers are perfectly happy with their end of the deal. They traded old for young. They got James on the minimum. They're 11-3. But Boston emerged with the player who has made a bigger difference thus far this season, and it got two first-round draft assets in the process. That doesn't mean the Celtics necessarily win the trade in the long run, but it does suggest, unsurprisingly, that Brad Stevens understood his own team and what it needed better than the rest of us.

Well, they haven't lost in three weeks... so this feels overdue. Let's talk about the much ballyhooed three-guard lineup for a moment. The Spurs couldn't keep bringing Dylan Harper off the bench this season. He's simply too good and too important to their future to risk alienating. They couldn't bench De'Aaron Fox immediately either. Former All-Stars tend to take such decisions as a sign of disrespect, and such a move could have splintered the locker room.

So the Spurs made the somewhat awkward decision to start the three of them together. The season's second game, a loss to the Houston Rockets, showcased exactly why so many feared the fit of the three of them together. Three iffy guard-sized shooters minimized spacing for the sake of redundant ball-handling, and the Harper-Fox-Stephon Castle trio got outscored by 12 points in a four-point defeat. Well, the three guards haven't lost their minutes together in a single game since then. They're +112 in 115 minutes after that point.

Now, there are notable caveats here. Every three-man combination of Spurs that has played at least 100 minutes since then is firmly positive, and the three guards have literally not played a single minute together this season that did not come alongside Victor Wembanyama. It's entirely possible that Wembanyama is so game-breaking that any lineup he's a part of is an almost automatic winner. But that would work in favor of the three guards here. Maybe San Antonio is so much more talented than the field that it can afford to play suboptimal lineups for the sake of maintaining harmony in the locker room.

That may prove more challenging late in a playoff series, but it's easier to convince players to change their roles for, say, Game 5 of the Western Conference Finals than it is in November or December. The Spurs might have to think harder about this in a field that included a healthy Oklahoma City, but with the Thunder compromised, San Antonio is such a large favorite to win the Western Conference that it can afford to try to just out-talent everyone else. So far, it's clearly working.

We are in all-out panic mode over the state of Cleveland's starting lineup. James Harden can't get to the rim anymore. Donovan Mitchell just signed a supermax extension that already feels iffy. Peyton Watson's shooting has fallen off a cliff and he's struggling as a primary point-of-attack defender. The Evan Mobley-Jarrett Allen partnership is getting crushed in its joint minutes. The starters have played 99 minutes together and lost those minutes by 24 points. No five-man unit that has played that many minutes has been outscored by more. Malaise doesn't do this core justice. Clearly, something here has to change.

Fortunately, there appear to be some internal solutions here. After FAA issues forced the Cavaliers to spend Friday night in Miami, Mitchell called for Saturday's game against the Dallas Mavericks to be postponed. The Cavaliers didn't arrive in Dallas until around noon on Saturday. The starters sat out. Cleveland won the game by 10 against a healthy, playoff-caliber opponent. Tyrese Proctor, Meleek Thomas, Mario Hezonja and Jaylon Tyson all scored between 18 and 24 points.

This wasn't a one-off. Thomas is outscoring Harden and Mobley on a per-minute basis. Proctor is sporting a better-than-6-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio on the season, and Synergy Sports rates him in the 100th percentile on spot-up efficiency and the 96th in pick-and-rolls, including passes, in terms of points per possession. Tyson breathes life into a transition offense that is otherwise a sore spot. Most of this team's energy comes from the bench.

What exactly the solution here is, we can't say. It will involve a trade. Perhaps a few. But there's something here, and the early indications are that things are going to get better for the team as a whole when it eventually starts leaning on these players a bit more.

Dejounte Murray requested a trade this week. That's not a rumor. The Pelicans publicly acknowledged it and Murray retweeted the news from ESPN. Meanwhile, after Monday's loss to the Golden State Warriors, Jordan Poole was asked if he would ever come back to the team with which he started his career. He answered "yes." Players tend to not be that definitive in those statements, nor do they tend to acknowledge that their former team "just feels like home." It certainly seems as though there's somewhere he'd rather be than New Orleans.

To borrow a phrase from social media user Nathan Calvin, "if you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two." Essentially... if two players seem this eager to flee, more probably do as well. Sam Amick suggested in a radio interview over the summer that Trey Murphy would like to play elsewhere. There has been plenty of speculation about other Pelicans as well. A 4-10 start following 26- and 21-win seasons tends to do that.

We're more than a year into Joe Dumars' reign as head of basketball operations and there's no discernible plan here. Virtually every key player from last year's roster was retained and the team has largely been healthier than it was a year ago, but they're on pace for a worse record under new head coach Jamahl Mosley. The sad thing is that the Pelicans have a fair number of valuable players. They've just assembled those players so carelessly that they've become far less than the sum of their parts. This team is incoherent, and even the players seem to know it.

Trae Young was held scoreless in 26 minutes on Sunday. It was the first time he's been held scoreless in his entire NBA career, but it may be the final straw of a trend that has been bubbling for some time: Trae Young is simply no longer a star-level scorer. He currently has his lowest shooting percentage from both 2-point and 3-point range in a single season. He lacks the burst to get to the rim or beat mismatches consistently anymore, and he's never developed comfort as a catch-and-shooter. Aside from free throws, it's basically all jumpers off the dribble and floaters, neither of which he's making at the rate he needs to in order to justify his defensive shortcomings. He scored 37 points against Detroit last Monday, but needed 17 free throws to get there on less than 35% shooting from the floor. He needs whistles right now.

This is a version of Young who probably shouldn't monopolize an offense, yet he's never shown that he's capable of playing differently. The Wizards are spending 26 possessions a game on shots Young generates either for himself or a teammate out of pick-and-roll, more than any other player in the league, per Synergy Sports. As of Sunday, he and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander were tied for the league lead among starters in average seconds possessing the ball per touch, per NBA.com tracking data. The younger players who represent the future of this organization are spending a whole lot of time watching someone else dribble. Nobody is really spacing the floor for anyone else since there's so little shooting on this roster. The Wizards have played close to neutral when Young rests, but are getting outscored by more than 10 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor. That difference is almost entirely offensive, yet Young remains the same defensive liability he's always been.

This is where the four-year max contract Washington bewilderingly gave Young becomes so destructive. The basic notion of acquiring a high-end point guard to serve as an offensive organizer for these young wings made sense on paper, but they committed to him essentially sight unseen. He played five mostly meaningless games in a tanking season and they paid him max money without really knowing how he'd fit with the team they were building. If he'd walked for nothing in free agency, well, it's not as though they spent picks to get him. Now they're stuck paying star-level money for a non-star-level player who probably can't meaningfully scale down his involvement in the offense because he just doesn't provide much value when any other player on either team has the basketball.

There are a lot of things going wrong in Washington right now, but Young is inevitably going to be the face of those struggles because he's the player the Wizards just bewilderingly gave a four-year max contract to in order to re-sign. Jaylen Brown had the loudest individual loss of the week, but he at least won all of his other games and has largely been what his team has asked him to be. Young went winless this week, had a scoreless game, and maintained his mostly disappointing season-long performance.

If you would have heard "the Warriors have a -2.4 net rating a month into the 2026-27 season," you probably would have shrugged and said, "sure, sounds about right." The Warriors were widely pegged as a low-end Play-In, high-end lottery team before the season, and a -2.4 net rating projects out to a win total in the 30s. Except that isn't Golden State's net rating. It's Golden State's net rating in the minutes Stephen Curry has missed this season.

That's how far above expectations Golden State was playing during its eight-game winning streak. The Curry-off version of the team was around average; the Curry-on version of the team was a juggernaut. The latter feels a bit unsustainable, but we won't know again for around a month. The former is what's about to be tested now that Curry has an oblique abdominal tear. The Spurs hardly represent a fair test for a team in this situation, but San Antonio predictably waxed Golden State by 38 in the first game of Curry's absence.

Nobody's asking for another eight-game winning streak. Those wins are banked, and Golden State's season begins in earnest when Jimmy Butler returns in January or February. For now, the Warriors just need to stay afloat. Find wins where the schedule offers them, and fortunately, the Pelicans, Kings, Clippers and Jazz are on the docket in the next three weeks or so. But losing Curry is a reminder of how fragile that streak really was. Maybe, now that Yaxel Lendeborg is emerging as a possible star, the Warriors are capable of genuine postseason success this season. But the health of any 38-year-old not named LeBron James is going to be precarious. Things could be a lot worse, but Curry's injury drags one of the feel-good stories of the early season back down to Earth.

#2705. Tari Eason gives amazing, blunt explanation for his 25-point game: 'S--t, the Wizards, for real'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Rockets improved to 11-3 on the season with a 147-119 beatdown of the Washington Wizards on Sunday night.

While Houston is no stranger to an offensive explosion, ranking second in the NBA this season in offensive rating (121.2), the 147 points scored on Sunday were 12 more than they've scored in a game this season. It was a balanced scoring effort as a team, as six players reached double figures and three scored at least 25 points -- including Tari Eason off the bench.

That 25-point performance represents a new season high for Eason -- his previous best was a 19-point effort against the Hawks -- as he went 10 for 14 from the field and 3 of 5 from 3-point range in 30 minutes off the bench. That effort earned Eason the honor of the walk-off TV interview, during which he gave a brutally honest (and hilarious) answer for why he was able to set a new season high and do so efficiently.

"Shit, the Wizards, for real. It was them," Eason said.

Tari Eason on what allowed him to have a season-high 25 points off the bench tonight:"Shit, the Wizards, for real." pic.twitter.com/t4bOwtzw5r

A+ work here, no notes. Eason could've puffed out his chest after beating up on the Wizards or complimented his teammates for allowing him to get in a rhythm, but instead chose the honest route rarely taken by players in a post-game interview and simply admitted that anyone could get buckets on Washington.

The Wizards are not the worst defense in the NBA -- that honor belongs to the Chicago Bulls -- but they are 25th in defensive rating and certainly do not boast very many elite defenders. Clearly, Eason didn't feel like he was doing anything special or out of the ordinary on Sunday night on his way to 25 points off the bench, and gave credit where it was due to the other team.

Unfortunately for the Wizards, it is not credit they'd like to take, and this feels like the kind of (earned) disrespect that should light some kind of fire under Washington.

#2703. Tang Kai Vs. Enkh-Orgil Baatarkhuu, Jonathan Di Bella Vs. Wang Junguang To Headline ONE 174: Shanghai

ONE Championship is heading back to China, and it is bringing a pair of massive World Title showdowns with it.

Reigning ONE Featherweight MMA World Champion Tang Kai defends his crown against former bantamweight MMA kingpin "The Tormentor" Enkh-Orgil Baatarkhuu in the main event, while Jonathan Di Bella puts his ONE Strawweight Kickboxing World Championship on the line against "The Warrior" Wang Junguang in the co-main event at ONE 174: Shanghai.

The blockbuster card goes down on Saturday, December 12, at Shanghai Indoor Stadium, marking the promotion's return to China for the first time in seven years.

Tang has been one of the most dominant forces in ONE Championship since the day he arrived. The 30-year-old Chinese superstar from Sunkin International Fight Club made history in 2022 when he outclassed then-champion Thanh Le to become China's first-ever male MMA World Champion — a World Title shot earned on the back of six consecutive victories following his 2019 promotional debut.

An injury briefly sidelined him, but he returned in 2024 to unify the division's belts against Le. After suffering a rare setback in a non-title bout, Tang rebounded in emphatic fashion to defend his crown against Shamil "The Cobra" Gasanov in May 2026.

The orthodox standout carries a 20-3 career record featuring 16 knockouts, an 80 percent finishing rate, and a 9-1 slate in ONE. Blending crisp, precision striking with stout wrestling and heavy ground-and-pound, he has already cleared out nearly every top contender in the division.

Now, he gets the chance to defend his gold in front of his compatriots, determined to deliver a showcase performance that makes his home country proud.

Standing across from him is a challenger who has spent months campaigning for this exact matchup. Enkh-Orgil Baatarkhuu, a 37-year-old representing Shandas MMA and Team Tungaa, recently became a breakout star on Netflix's Physical: Asia.

He won six of his first seven ONE outings to earn a bantamweight MMA title shot, then submitted Fabricio "Wonder Boy" Andrade in the fourth round in December 2025 to make history for Mongolia. After dropping the belt in his first defense earlier this year, Baatarkhuu now moves up a weight class with two clear objectives in sight.

The Mongolian veteran aims to claim the featherweight crown once held by his mentor, Narantungalag "Tungaa" Jadambaa, and become Mongolia's first two-division MMA World Champion. Armed with a 14-4 record and a 7-2 ONE ledger, he smothers opponents with dirty boxing, turns the clinch into a grueling battle, and finishes the job on the canvas.

Five-time ONE Strawweight Kickboxing World Champion Jonathan Di Bella looks to add another high-profile World Title defense to his near-flawless resume.

The 30-year-old Canadian-Italian southpaw from Team Di Bella Kickboxing is a lightning-fast technician who pairs a Kyokushin karate foundation with some of the slickest boxing in the sport. He enters Shanghai with a 16-1 career record, a 6-1 mark in ONE, and a four-fight winning streak.

His ONE journey began in 2022, when he captured the vacant strawweight kickboxing crown against Chinese phenom "Fighting Rooster" Zhang Peimian in his promotional debut. After vacating the belt due to illness on weigh-in day ahead of a scheduled 2024 defense, he suffered his lone career defeat to Prajanchai Pongsuphan PK for the vacant strap that June.

Di Bella wasted no time climbing back to the summit, however, winning the interim belt in 2025 against the legendary Sam-A Gaiyanghadao before unifying the belts against Prajanchai to become undisputed champion and avenge his only loss. In his most recent outing, he successfully turned back Zhang once again.

Wang, meanwhile, steps into a rare opportunity to claim the very belt he first chased seven years ago.

The 31-year-old from Liu Xiangming Fight Club made an electric start to his promotional tenure and challenged Sam-A for the inaugural ONE Strawweight Kickboxing World Championship — a crown that slipped through his fingers by the slimmest of margins.

Following nearly six years away, the high-volume, boxing-heavy striker returned in October and stunned the combat sports world by defeating ONE Strawweight Muay Thai World Champion Prajanchai under kickboxing rules. Now, carrying a 31-7 career record, Wang gets his long-awaited second crack at the gold — and this time, he intends to leave the Circle with it.
